q: How do interviewers judge communication in a coding round?
plain: They judge whether they could follow your reasoning without having to ask. Rubrics separate candidates the interviewer followed with no effort from those who needed follow up questions and those who jumped into code without explaining. Done well sounds like: 'Let me restate it, then I'll give two approaches before I code.' Done badly sounds like typing in silence for five minutes and then saying 'okay, I think this works'. The second candidate may have the same solution, but the interviewer cannot write down how they got there.
deep: The Tech Interview Handbook's rubric has four dimensions: communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing. Communication bands: strong hire (thorough, organised, succinct; the interviewer had no trouble following), leaning hire (clear, but the interviewer asked follow ups to understand the approach), leaning no hire (insufficient, for example coding without explaining, or disorganised), strong no hire (silent even when addressed). Behaviours that move you up: restating the problem, asking two or three clarifying questions, discussing approaches and trade offs before coding, narrating intent while coding, and testing aloud.
say: They're judging whether they could follow my reasoning without having to pull it out of me. The rubrics I've read separate a candidate the interviewer followed with no effort from one they had to keep asking 'what do you mean?', and from one who jumped into code without explaining. So I make the plan visible: I restate the problem, ask a couple of clarifying questions, say two approaches and their trade offs, get a go ahead, then narrate what each block is for. The trade off is time, so I narrate decisions, not keystrokes. And I test out loud before saying I'm done.
must_mention: approaches and trade offs before code

followups.q: What's the most common communication failure?
followups.a: Jumping into code before explaining the approach, which is the leaning no hire row.

followups.q: Is silence ever fine?
followups.a: A short announced silence, yes: 'give me thirty seconds to think about the invariant.'

traps: Thinking communication means talking constantly.
Treating communication as charm instead of followability.

q: If I ask you 'what is dropout?', how do you decide how much to say?
plain: Answer in layers: one sentence that answers it, about 30 seconds of intuition and example, then offer to go deeper. The interviewer's reaction tells you whether they want more. Done well: 'Dropout randomly switches off units during training so the network can't rely on any one of them. Want the maths or the failure modes?' Done badly: a four minute tour of the original paper before the definition arrives. The interviewer's time is a budget, and the headline spends it carefully.
deep: Layers: headline (one sentence, the definition with its category), short (30 seconds: one mechanism and one example), medium (2 minutes: how it works, the main trade off, failure modes), deep dive on request (derivation, edge cases, numbers). For dropout: headline 'randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit'; short: ensemble of thinned networks sharing weights, inverted scaling so inference needs no change; medium: interaction with batch norm, use in large pretrained models, Monte Carlo dropout. The explicit offer ('maths or failure modes?') converts guessing into a choice the interviewer makes.
say: I answer in layers and let the interviewer choose the depth. One sentence first: dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training so the network can't rely on any single unit. Then about thirty seconds: it behaves like training many thinned networks that share weights, and with inverted dropout you scale during training so inference needs no change. Then I stop and offer: I can go into why the scaling preserves the expectation, or into when it hurts, like with batch norm. That pause matters, because if they wanted a quick check I haven't spent four minutes of their plan.
must_mention: about 30 seconds of intuition and example
explicit offer of the next layer

followups.q: What if they say 'go deeper'?
followups.a: Give the 2 minute layer: mechanism, trade off, failure mode, then offer the derivation.

followups.q: What's the failure mode of layering?
followups.a: Stopping at the headline when depth was wanted. The explicit offer prevents that.

traps: Starting with the history of the technique.
Delivering the deep dive unprompted.

q: Give me the bias variance trade off in one sentence, then thirty seconds, then two minutes.
plain: A drill for layering. One sentence: simple models miss patterns, complex models chase noise, and you want the balance that predicts new data best. Then add an example, then the mechanism and how you would detect each problem. Done well, the 10 second version already contains the answer and each longer version adds one new idea. Done badly, the 30 second version is the same definition said more slowly. Practising all three lengths of one answer is the fastest way to build the habit.
deep: Headline: expected test error splits into bias squared, variance and irreducible noise, and model complexity trades the first two. 30 seconds: a straight line underfits a curved relationship (high bias); a degree 15 polynomial on 20 points fits the noise (high variance). 2 minutes: diagnose with learning curves (high bias: train and validation error both high and close; high variance: large gap); fixes (more features or capacity for bias; more data, regularisation, bagging for variance); caveat that very large overparameterised networks can show double descent, so the classical U curve is not the whole story.
say: In one sentence: test error comes from bias, variance and noise, and model complexity trades bias against variance. In thirty seconds: a straight line on curved data misses the pattern, that's bias, while a very wiggly polynomial on twenty points memorises the noise, that's variance. In two minutes I'd add how I diagnose it: if training and validation error are both high and close, it's bias, so I add capacity or features; if there's a big gap, it's variance, so I add data or regularisation or average models. And I'd flag the caveat that very large networks can show double descent, so the U curve isn't the whole story.
must_mention: each layer answers on its own
a concrete example in the 30 second layer

followups.q: Why practise three lengths?
followups.a: So the 10 second version always contains the answer and you can stop at any layer.

traps: A 30 second layer that is only a longer definition with no example.

q: How do you structure an answer to 'explain X'?
plain: Use five moves in a fixed order: what it is, the intuition, a concrete example, the trade off, and when you would use it. The order matters because the first sentence answers the question and each later move adds one new kind of evidence. Done well, 'explain BM25' starts 'BM25 is a keyword ranking function that scores documents by term frequency, damped and length normalised', then gives the intuition, an example and its weakness. Done badly, it starts with the history of TF-IDF and never reaches the trade off. The template works for any concept on your resume.
deep:
| Move | Says | Common miss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | One sentence with the category | Starting with history |
| Intuition | Mechanism or analogy in plain words | Analogy that breaks at the edges, unflagged |
| Example | Numbers, a tiny case, your own work | Staying abstract |
| Trade off | Cost, assumption, failure mode | Presenting it as free |
| When to use | Decision rule against the alternative | Never naming the alternative |

Research interviewers follow almost every concept answer with 'when does it fail?' and 'what would you use instead?', so the last two moves pre load the follow ups.
say: I use the same five moves every time. First what it is, in one sentence with its category, so the question is answered immediately. Then the intuition, the mechanism in plain words. Then a concrete example, ideally with numbers or from my own work. Then the trade off, what it costs or when it breaks. And finally when I'd use it and what I'd use instead. For BM25 that's: a keyword ranking function; it rewards rare terms and damps repeated ones; it beat DPR and TAS-B on SciFact in the BEIR paper; it misses synonyms; so I pair it with a dense retriever. The last two moves are where follow ups land.
must_mention: when to use and the alternative

followups.q: Why this order?
followups.a: The definition answers the question; each later move adds a different kind of evidence, and the last two pre answer the usual follow ups.

followups.q: What if they cut you off after the definition?
followups.a: Good, they had what they needed; the layered answer lets them stop you.

traps: Starting with the history of the idea.
Skipping the trade off.

q: Explain overfitting to a product manager with no ML background.
plain: Use the five step template: what it is, an intuition, an example, the cost, and what you would do about it, in everyday words. Done well, every term is one the PM could repeat to their own manager. Done badly, the answer says 'high variance on held out data' and the PM nods without understanding. The test is whether your listener could explain it back.
deep: Template: what it is (a model that memorises its training data, including the noise, so it does worse on new data); intuition (a student who memorises past exam answers instead of learning the method); example (98 percent accuracy on data it has seen, 70 percent on new customers); trade off (more complex models fit more but generalise worse past a point); when to act (always measure on held out data the model never saw, and prefer the simpler model when they score similarly). Feynman test: every term must be one the PM could repeat.
say: Overfitting is when a model memorises its training data, quirks included, so it looks great on data it's seen and disappoints on new data. It's like a student who memorises last year's exam answers: perfect on the practice test, lost when the questions change. A concrete version is a churn model that's 98 percent accurate on last year's customers and much worse on this month's. The trade off is that flexible models can learn more but also memorise more. What we do about it is always score the model on data it never saw, and if two models score about the same there, we ship the simpler one.
must_mention: held out evaluation as the fix

followups.q: How would you know it's happening?
followups.a: A large gap between training and held out performance.

followups.q: What if the PM asks how much data is enough?
followups.a: Show a learning curve: if held out performance still rises with more data, more data helps.

traps: Using jargon like 'variance' without defining it.
No example.

q: Explain reciprocal rank fusion and when you'd use it.
plain: RRF merges several ranked lists by giving each document points based on its rank in each list, so documents that several systems rank highly win. It ignores raw scores, which helps when systems score on different scales. Done well, the answer names the alternative (a learned weighted fusion) and when it would win. Done badly, it says 'it combines the results' with no mechanism and no cost.
deep: Definition: $\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_r 1/(k + \text{rank}_r(d))$, usually $k = 60$ (Cormack and colleagues, 2009). Intuition: rewards agreement near the top; rank based, so no score calibration between BM25 and cosine. Example: ranked 1st and 3rd gives $1/61 + 1/63 \approx 0.0323$; 2nd and 1st gives $\approx 0.0325$. Trade off: discards magnitude, so a very confident retriever gets no extra weight; a document missing from one list loses that term. When: default fusion of lexical and dense retrieval. In the BEIR replication, hybrid RRF over BM25 and TAS-B scored 0.687 nDCG@10 on SciFact against 0.677 (BM25) and 0.643 (TAS-B), labelled as not in the paper.
say: Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists by giving each document one over sixty plus its rank in each list and summing. The intuition is that documents several retrievers rank near the top are usually good, and because it only uses ranks, I never have to calibrate BM25 scores against cosine similarities. For example, ranked first and third beats appearing in only one list. The trade off is that it throws away score magnitude, so a very confident dense model gets no extra say. I use it as the default for hybrid search; in my BEIR replication it beat both of its inputs on SciFact.
must_mention: sum of one over k plus rank
hybrid default; beat both inputs on SciFact

followups.q: When would you use a learned fusion instead?
followups.a: When you have relevance labels to fit weights and the score distributions are stable.

followups.q: What does k do?
followups.a: Larger k flattens the difference between top ranks; smaller k rewards the very top more.

traps: Saying RRF averages scores.

q: What is the Feynman technique and how do you use it to prepare?
plain: The Feynman technique is a study method: you explain an idea in words a 12 year old could follow, and wherever your simple explanation breaks, you have found a gap. Farnam Street describes four steps: map what you know, explain it simply, go back to the source wherever you got stuck, then test yourself by teaching it without notes. For interviews, the place where your simple version needs an undefined term is exactly where the follow up question will land. For example, if you cannot explain nDCG without saying 'discounted gain', you need to learn what is being discounted and why. Done well, you finish with a short explanation you could say aloud; done badly, you reread the paper and feel familiar with it.
deep: Steps (Farnam Street): (1) select a concept and write everything you know; (2) explain it as if to a 12 year old; (3) review and refine, returning to the source where the explanation fails; (4) test by teaching someone without notes, then archive the simple explanation for review. Interview use: run it on every concept on your resume, and on every number in your project stories (what is it out of, how was it measured). The mechanism is that jargon can hide a missing understanding; plain words cannot.
say: It's a study method where I explain a concept in words a twelve year old would follow, and wherever the simple version breaks, I've found a gap in my understanding. The steps are: write down what I know, explain it simply, go back to the source wherever I got stuck, and then test it by teaching someone without notes. I use it on every concept on my resume. For example, explaining nDCG simply forced me to say what exactly gets discounted, which is the gain of a relevant document, by the log of its rank. The place my plain explanation breaks is usually exactly where the interviewer's follow up will land.

followups.q: How is that different from rereading?
followups.a: Rereading builds recognition; explaining builds recall and exposes gaps.

followups.q: Who do you practise on?
followups.a: A non technical friend, noting every term they stop you on.

traps: Using a simple analogy that is wrong at the edges and not saying so.

q: How do you keep a long technical answer easy to follow?
plain: Signpost the structure, keep one claim per sentence, pause after each key point, replace filler with a short silence, and repeat the headline at the end. Done well, the listener hears structure, pauses and a repeated headline. Done badly, one long sentence joined by 'and um so basically' runs for a minute.
deep: Techniques: announce structure ('two parts'); short sentences, since fillers cluster at clause boundaries; deliberate pauses after claims the interviewer might write down; slower than conversational pace, especially in the first five minutes when nerves speed people up; hedges only for real uncertainty; repeat the headline at the end. Winston's observation, as reported, is that at any moment part of an audience has drifted, so key ideas need repeating.
say: I tell them the structure up front, like 'there are two parts to this', so they know when one part ends. I keep sentences short, one claim each, and pause after anything they might want to write down. When I feel a filler word coming, I let a second of silence happen instead, which sounds like thinking rather than nerves. I save hedges for things I'm actually unsure about. And at the end of a long answer I repeat the headline in one sentence, because some of what I said will have been missed while they were writing.

followups.q: How do you practise?
followups.a: Record answers and count fillers per minute; repeat with the instruction to pause instead.

traps: Speeding up when nervous.

q: What do you say in the first two minutes after I give you a coding problem?
plain: Restate the problem, ask two or three clarifying questions, check a tiny example, then describe a simple approach and a better one with their costs, and ask before you start coding. Each clarifying question should change your solution if answered differently. A tiny worked example agreed with the interviewer is the cheapest insurance against solving the wrong problem.
deep: Sequence from the Tech Interview Handbook checklist: paraphrase the question; ask at least two or three clarifications (input size and range, sorted or not, duplicates, empty input, may I mutate); work a small example and confirm expected output; describe a brute force and an optimised approach at a high level with time and space complexity; agree on one; get a green light. Candidates who skip this and code immediately land in the leaning no hire communication band.
say: First I restate the problem in my own words, because that catches a misunderstanding in five seconds. Then two or three clarifying questions: how big the input is, whether it can be empty or have duplicates, whether it's sorted, whether I can modify it. I check one tiny example with the interviewer so we agree on the output. Then I describe two approaches, usually the brute force and a faster one, with their time and space costs, say which I'd pick and why, and ask if that sounds good before I write anything. It costs a couple of minutes and saves the fifteen I'd lose solving the wrong problem.

followups.q: What if the interviewer says 'just start'?
followups.a: Say the approach in one sentence anyway, then start.

followups.q: How many clarifying questions is too many?
followups.a: More than a handful; ask the ones that change the solution and state assumptions for the rest.

traps: Coding immediately.
Asking questions whose answers would not change the solution.

q: You're stuck halfway through a coding problem. What do you do?
plain: Keep narrating: say what you know, what you are trying, and where it breaks. That lets the interviewer give a small hint. A short announced pause is fine; long silence is not. Done well: 'I'm stuck on removing the second pass; I know the output is sorted, so let me test building it in place.' Done badly: two minutes of silence, then a guess.
deep: Script: name the sticking point precisely ('I need to avoid the second pass'); list the facts you have ('output order matches sorted order'); propose a candidate and test it on the example aloud; if it fails, say why. Fall back to the brute force if time is short and say you will optimise after. Interviewers would rather give a small hint than watch silence, and voicing a half formed idea often prompts it. Announce any silence ('give me thirty seconds').
say: I keep talking, but about the search, not the panic. I'd say exactly where I'm stuck, for example that I can't see how to avoid a second pass, then what I do know, like that the output follows the sorted order, and then try a candidate idea on the example out loud. If it breaks, I say why it breaks. That gives the interviewer something to nudge, and a small hint is much better for both of us than two minutes of silence. If I need to think quietly, I say 'give me thirty seconds', and if time is short I'll get the brute force working first and say I'll optimise after.
must_mention: fall back to brute force if needed

followups.q: Does taking a hint hurt you?
followups.a: A small hint costs less than silence or a wrong solution, and how you use it is itself a signal.

traps: Going silent for minutes.
Pretending to be fine and coding something you know is wrong.

q: You've finished writing the code. What now?
plain: Do not say 'done'. Read your code for mistakes, trace a small example out loud while tracking the variables, try edge cases, then restate the complexity and what you would improve. Done well: tracing a three element example aloud and catching an off by one error yourself. Done badly: saying 'done' and waiting for the interviewer to find the bug.
deep: Handbook checklist after coding: scan for off by one errors as if reading someone else's code; step through a test case updating state like a debugger; brainstorm edge cases (empty, single element, duplicates, negatives, very large); fix bugs calmly in place; restate time and space complexity; mention refactors or improvements given more time. Announcing completion first is listed as a mistake, and self corrected bugs count in the testing dimension.
say: I don't announce I'm done. I reread the code as if someone else wrote it, looking for off by one errors, then trace a small example out loud, saying the value of each variable as it changes. Then I try the awkward inputs: empty, a single element, duplicates, something large. If I find a bug I say so and fix it in place, which interviewers tend to read as a good sign. Finally I restate the time and space complexity and say what I'd change with more time, like input validation I skipped.

followups.q: What edge cases do you always try?
followups.a: Empty input, one element, duplicates, extremes of range, and the case the problem statement hints at.

traps: Saying 'I think it works' without tracing.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview cheatsheet

q: How do you narrate a derivation so the interviewer can check each step?
plain: Treat it as a short story: goal first, symbols defined, one step at a time with the reason it is allowed, the result in words, then a check with a number or a limiting case. Done well: 'Goal: the gradient. Symbols: x, y, p. Step one uses the chain rule.' Done badly: writing silently for three minutes and turning around with an answer nobody can verify.
deep: Five moves: goal; symbols (written and said); steps each with a named rule (chain rule, linearity of expectation, independence assumption); result restated in words; sanity check (units, a limiting case, a two value numeric example). Board management: goal boxed, permanent definitions column, numbered lines for reference, space between lines for inserted steps. Say assumptions before using them, since 'what assumption did you just make?' is the standard follow up. Verbalise formulas ('one over the length of the response') instead of notation.
say: I treat it like a short story with a fixed plot. I say the goal first, so they know where I'm heading. I define every symbol out loud and write it in a corner I won't erase. Then one step at a time, naming the rule that makes it legal, like the chain rule or an independence assumption, and I say the assumption before I use it. At the end I say the result in plain words and check it, with a limiting case or two quick numbers. I number the lines so I can say 'from line three', and if I slip, I fix it in place and say so.
must_mention: name the rule for each step
check with a number or limit

followups.q: What if you forget a step?
followups.a: Say what you need to be true and ask to treat it as given, then continue.

traps: Erasing definitions to make room.

q: Derive the gradient of the logistic loss and talk me through it.
plain: State the goal, define each symbol, take each step with its reason, say the result in words, then check a simple case. The result is the prediction error times the input. The whole derivation fits in four lines, and the narration is what makes it checkable. Done badly, the symbols appear on the board with no definitions and the interviewer is lost by the second line.
deep: Goal: $\partial \ell / \partial w$. Symbols: $p = \sigma(w^\top x)$, $y \in \{0,1\}$. Loss $\ell = -y\log p - (1-y)\log(1-p)$. Using $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$: $\partial\ell/\partial p = -y/p + (1-y)/(1-p)$, $\partial p/\partial w = p(1-p)x$, product $(p - y)x$. Check: $p = y$ gives zero gradient; sign: if $p > y$ the update $w \leftarrow w - \eta(p-y)x$ lowers $w^\top x$. Narration habits: goal boxed at top, definitions column, numbered lines, fix slips in place.
say: I want the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights. Let me define things: x is the input, y is the label, zero or one, and p is the sigmoid of w dot x. The loss is minus y log p minus one minus y times log one minus p. I'll use the fact that the sigmoid's derivative is sigma times one minus sigma. Chain rule: the derivative with respect to p, times p times one minus p times x, and the terms cancel to p minus y, times x. In words, the update is the prediction error times the input. Sanity check: if p equals y, the gradient is zero, which is right.
must_mention: result p minus y times x

followups.q: Why does the cross entropy pair so nicely with the sigmoid?
followups.a: The p times one minus p from the sigmoid cancels the denominators from the log terms, leaving a linear error term.

followups.q: What about a batch?
followups.a: Average the per example gradients: X transpose times p minus y, divided by n.

traps: Reading LaTeX aloud.
Skipping the definitions and losing the interviewer at line two.

q: Design a RAG question answering service. Where do you start?
plain: Say your plan for the round first, then gather the top requirements with quantified qualities, list the core entities, sketch the API, build a simple end to end design, and save time for deep dives on the weakest parts. Done well, the first minute is a spoken plan and two or three questions. Done badly, the first minute is 'so I'd use Pinecone' before anyone knows what the system is for.
deep: Opening: 'I'll do requirements, core entities, API, a simple end to end design, then deep dives.' Requirements: users can ask a question and get an answer with citations; can see sources; admins can add documents. Quantify: p95 latency, freshness of new documents, cost per query. Entities: Document, Chunk, Query, Answer, Citation. API: POST /ask, POST /documents. High level: ingest and chunk, hybrid retrieval (BM25 plus dense, RRF), rerank, generate with citations, verify citations. Deep dives: evaluation, stale or invalid documents (EvidenceOps resolves trust at query time), cost. Skip upfront estimates unless they decide something (for example index memory).
say: I'd start by saying my plan: requirements, the core entities, the API, a simple design that works end to end, and then deep dives on the weakest parts. For requirements I'd ask who the users are and what the corpus is, and pin numbers like a latency budget and how fresh new documents must be. Entities are documents, chunks, queries, answers and citations. The API is basically ask and add documents. Then a simple path: chunk and index, hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, rerank, generate with a citation on each claim, verify the citations. Then I'd check in: evaluation or handling documents that become invalid, which would you like first?

followups.q: What would you deep dive first?
followups.a: Evaluation, because every later decision needs a way to measure it.

followups.q: How do you handle a document that becomes invalid?
followups.a: Resolve its status at query time from a registry, as in EvidenceOps, so no reindex is needed.

traps: Starting with vector database choice before requirements.
Adding caching and sharding before a working path exists.

source.title: Hello Interview: delivery framework

q: How do you keep a 45 minute design round on track?
plain: Announce the phases and rough times at the start, signpost each transition, check in at boundaries, and get a simple working design before adding complexity. Done well, the interviewer always knows which phase you are in because you said so. Done badly, you are still estimating storage at minute twenty and never reach a working design.
deep: Hello Interview's delivery framework: requirements about 5 minutes (top three functional requirements, three to five quantified non functional ones), core entities briefly, API about 5 minutes, high level design in the middle block, deep dives in the last 10 or so minutes. It names failing to deliver a working system as the most common mid level failure, often recorded as time management. Signposts ('that's requirements; moving to the API') let the interviewer redirect at boundaries. Seniority shows in leading the deep dives yourself.
say: I make the plan visible at the start: about five minutes on requirements, a couple on the main entities, five on the API, the middle on a simple design that works end to end, and the last ten or so on deep dives. Then I signpost every transition, like 'that's requirements, moving to the API', and check in at the boundaries, which lets the interviewer redirect me without interrupting. The rule I hold myself to is a working path before any complexity, because the most common way to fail these rounds is never finishing. If I see two weak spots, I name both and ask which to take first.

followups.q: What if the interviewer drags you into detail early?
followups.a: Answer briefly, note it as a deep dive candidate, and return to the plan.

traps: Spending 20 minutes on requirements and estimates.

source.title: Hello Interview: delivery framework

q: Why did you pick that component over the alternative?
plain: Give the reason tied to a requirement, and the condition under which you would choose differently. Interviewers grade whether you know what the choice depends on. Done well: 'I chose a queue because bursts happen; if load were tiny, I'd call the scorer directly.' Done badly: 'Kafka is the industry standard.'
deep: The interviewing.io guide: interviewers want well reasoned, qualified decisions based on trade offs, with an explanation of how they would change under different circumstances. Pattern: 'I picked X because requirement R and access pattern A; the cost is C; if R changed to R prime, I would switch to Y.' Example: a queue between ingestion and scoring because the scorer can lag and bursts happen; cost is eventual consistency of predictions; for very low volume a direct call is simpler.
say: I'd tie it to a requirement and then say when I'd change my mind. For example, I put a queue between ingestion and the scorer because alerts arrive in bursts and the scorer can fall behind, so the queue absorbs the burst without dropping anything. The cost is that predictions land a little later and the system is eventually consistent. If the volume were tiny and latency mattered more than resilience, I'd call the scorer directly and skip the extra moving part. I try to give every choice that shape, reason, cost and switching condition, because the choice matters less than knowing what it depends on.

followups.q: What if they prefer the alternative?
followups.a: Ask which requirement they are weighting, then show how the design changes.

traps: Defending a choice with 'it's the industry standard'.

source.title: interviewing.io: system design interview guide

q: Daily active users dropped 10 percent yesterday. Walk me through it.
plain: Say a structure first: clarify the metric and comparison, rule out a measurement problem, look at the shape of the drop, find the segment where it concentrates, rank hypotheses with the data that would test each, and recommend an action. Done well, the structure is said before any guess and the first check is whether the data is right. Done badly, the first sentence is 'probably a competitor launched something'.
deep: Clarify: definition of active, the comparison (day over day, same weekday last week), size relative to normal variation. Measurement: logging changes, pipeline delays, a deploy, timezone or definition changes; check a second source like server logs. Shape: a step at one hour suggests a release or outage; a gradual slide suggests product or external causes. Segment: platform, app version, country, new versus returning, acquisition channel; aggregates can hide opposite moves. Hypotheses: ranked by likelihood and cost to check, each with the confirming cut. Recommend: rollback if a release, or monitor with a threshold that would trigger action.
say: First I'd pin down what dropped: how active is defined, and compared with what, because a Sunday against a Saturday is a different story from a week over week drop. Then I'd rule out measurement, a logging change, a late pipeline or a definition change, since that's often the real answer. Next the shape: a sudden step at one hour points to a release or outage, a slow slide to product or outside causes. Then segment by platform, app version, country and new versus returning users to see where it concentrates. I'd rank two or three hypotheses with the cut that confirms each, and end with a recommendation.

followups.q: Which segment first?
followups.a: Platform and app version, because a release is the most common sudden cause and it is cheap to check.

followups.q: What if no segment stands out?
followups.a: Look for an external cause such as a holiday or competitor event, and compare with last year.

traps: Jumping to a cause before checking the data is right.
Listing a dozen causes with no order.

q: How would you measure whether a new feature is successful?
plain: State what the feature is for, pick one main metric that shows that goal, add two or three guardrails that must not get worse, and say how you would test it and what result would stop the launch. Done well, the primary metric follows from the feature's purpose. Done badly, the metric is clicks on the new button, which says people found it, not that it helped them.
deep: Structure: goal in one sentence; user action that shows the goal; primary metric (sensitive, attributable, aligned with long term value); guardrails (latency, retention, revenue, support tickets); test design (randomised experiment, unit of randomisation, duration covering weekly cycles, power); decision rule including what would block launch; novelty effects. The experimentation module on this site carries the statistics.
say: I'd start with what the feature is for in one sentence, because the metric falls out of that. Say it's saved searches: the goal is getting people back to listings faster, so the main metric might be returning sessions that reach a listing, not clicks on the save button. Then two or three guardrails that must not get worse, like page latency and overall retention. I'd test it with a randomised experiment at the user level, long enough to cover weekly cycles, and decide before launch what result would stop it. The trade off is that the cleanest metric is often slower to move, so I'd pair it with a faster leading indicator.

followups.q: Why not use feature usage as the metric?
followups.a: Usage shows adoption, not value; it can rise while the outcome you care about falls.

traps: Choosing a vanity metric like clicks on the new button.

q: Build a model to predict customer churn. Go.
plain: Before modelling, ask the two or three questions that change the answer: what counts as churn, what decision the prediction drives, and what data and timing you have. Then state assumptions for the rest. Done well, three questions that each change the model or the metric. Done badly, either no questions or ten questions and no start.
deep: High value clarifications: churn definition and horizon (cancel within 30 days? inactivity?), the action taken on predictions (retention offer, so precision at top k matters), data available at prediction time (to avoid leakage), base rate, latency (batch weekly versus real time), how success is measured (uplift from the intervention, not only AUC). State assumptions aloud so they can be corrected. Paraphrase back first.
say: Before I pick a model I'd ask three things. What counts as churn, cancelling within thirty days or going inactive? What will we do with the prediction, because if it triggers a retention offer, what matters is precision among the people we contact, not overall accuracy. And what data exists at the moment we'd predict, so I don't train on anything that leaks the outcome. For everything else I'd state assumptions, say a weekly batch score and a churn rate around a few percent, and you can correct me. Then I'd start with a simple baseline before anything fancy.

followups.q: Why ask about the decision?
followups.a: It chooses the metric: a retention offer budget means precision at top k.

followups.q: What leakage would you watch for?
followups.a: Features recorded after the cancellation, like a closed account flag.

traps: Jumping to model choice.
Asking ten questions and never starting.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview cheatsheet

q: What clarifying questions do you ask in an ML system design round?
plain: Questions that change the design: the product goal, where labels come from, latency and cost budgets, online versus batch, how success is measured offline and online, and what an error costs. Done well, each question changes a design choice. Done badly, the questions are generic ('how many users?') and the answers are never used.
deep: Goal and success metric (online), label source and delay, data volume and freshness, latency budget per request, cost per request, batch or online inference, fairness or safety constraints, cost of false positives versus false negatives, existing systems to integrate with. The interviewing.io guide warns against assuming the familiar product version (rebuilding Instagram for 'a photo service'); ask what kind of system they mean.
say: I ask the questions that would change the design. What's the product goal and the online metric we'll be judged on? Where do labels come from and how delayed are they, since click labels arrive in seconds and fraud labels in weeks? What's the latency and cost budget per request, and is inference online or batch? And what does each kind of error cost, because that sets the threshold and the evaluation. I keep it to three or four, then say my assumptions for the rest, like 'I'll assume 200 milliseconds and a million requests a day unless you say otherwise.'

followups.q: What if the interviewer says 'you decide'?
followups.a: State a reasonable assumption, say why, and move on.

traps: Assuming the most famous version of the product.

source.title: interviewing.io: system design interview guide

q: Have you worked with ColBERT's late interaction scoring?
plain: If you have not, say so, then say what you do know about it, give a labelled guess, and say how you would check. That turns a gap into evidence of how you reason. Done well, you say 'not directly' in the first three words and then show what you do know. Done badly, you bluff a definition and the next question exposes it.
deep: Script: boundary ('not directly'); adjacent knowledge (ColBERT keeps one embedding per token and scores with a sum over query tokens of the maximum similarity to any document token, so its index is much larger than a single vector model's); labelled hypothesis (token level matching may help rare scientific terms; BEIR reported ColBERT at 0.671 nDCG@10 on SciFact against BM25's 0.665); plan (read the scoring function, run on one dataset against a single vector baseline). Calibrate confidence words.
say: Not directly, no. What I know is that it keeps one embedding per token instead of one per document, and scores a query by summing, over query tokens, the best match among the document's tokens, which is why its index is much bigger than a single vector model's. In the BEIR paper it was slightly ahead of BM25 on SciFact, if I remember right. My guess is token level matching helps with rare scientific terms, but that's a hypothesis. If I needed it, I'd read the scoring function and run it on SciFact against bge-small, since I already have that harness from my replication.

followups.q: Why not just bluff?
followups.a: The next question lands exactly where a bluff breaks, and it costs trust for the rest of the loop.

traps: Saying 'I don't know' and stopping.
Inventing a benchmark number.

q: How do you answer when you only half remember a number?
plain: Give the direction and the source, say you are not sure of the exact figure, and offer to check. Never fill the gap with a made up number. Done well: 'TAS-B was a couple of points behind BM25 on SciFact; I'd check the exact figure.' Done badly: confidently stating a number you half remember.
deep: Pattern: direction plus provenance plus confidence ('TAS-B was close to BM25 on SciFact in the BEIR paper; I don't remember the exact figure'). For your own projects, know every number with its denominator and caveat; interviewers sometimes ask a number back later, and a changed number costs credibility. Calibrated language ('I'm sure', 'I believe, but I'd verify', 'I'm guessing') makes your sure claims worth more.
say: I give the direction and where it came from, and I say plainly that I don't have the exact figure. Something like: 'In the BEIR paper, TAS-B was close to BM25 on SciFact, a couple of points behind, but I'd want to check the exact number.' That's still useful to the interviewer, and it keeps my other numbers credible. The one place I don't allow myself this is my own projects: there I know every number, what it's out of and its caveat, because interviewers sometimes ask a number back twenty minutes later to see if it changes.

followups.q: What if they press for a number?
followups.a: Give a range you are confident in and label it as approximate.

traps: Rounding a half memory into a precise figure.

q: I don't think your approach will scale. Convince me.
plain: Restate their concern, find out what assumption it rests on, then either update and show what changes or explain your reasoning and when you would change your mind. Done well, you restate the concern before answering it. Done badly, you either cave instantly or argue past the point they actually made.
deep: Three moves: restate ('so the worry is the lookup on every request adds latency'); classify (new information, different assumption, or a test of conviction; ask if unclear: 'is it p99 you are worried about?'); respond on merits (concede and adapt with a concrete change, or hold with a reason and a switching condition). Amazon's 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit' covers respectful challenge then full commitment. Changing your mind for a good reason is a positive signal.
say: Let me make sure I have the concern: is it the trust lookup on every request adding latency at high traffic? If so, the registry is thousands of rows held in memory, so the lookup is microseconds, and I'd keep it. But you're right that it's a dependency on the serving path. If the registry moved to a remote service, I'd cache it locally with a short time to live and accept a few minutes of staleness. And if it outgrew memory, I'd revisit the design. So I'd hold the approach for now, and here's the condition under which I'd change it.

followups.q: What if you realise they're right?
followups.a: Say so directly and show what changes; that is a positive signal.

traps: Folding immediately.
Arguing without restating their point.

q: I think your answer is wrong.
plain: Check it out loud instead of either folding or arguing: test the claim on an example and let the evidence decide. Done well, a live trace settles it in thirty seconds. Done badly, you change a correct answer because the interviewer sounded sure.
deep: Interviewers sometimes push back on correct answers to test conviction. The Handbook advises not arguing with a coding interviewer since they know the question well; the useful middle path is a live check: 'Let me trace it with the empty input... it returns an empty list, as required.' If the trace reveals a bug, concede and fix. Phrases: 'You're right, I missed that'; 'I see it differently, and here's the assumption I'm making'.
say: I'd check it in front of them rather than argue or fold. Something like: 'Let me trace it with the case you're worried about.' Then I walk the input through the code out loud. If it does break, I say 'you're right, I missed that', and fix it. If it holds, I show the trace and ask whether there's a case I haven't considered, because sometimes the interviewer has a specific input in mind. Either way the evidence decides, not my ego, and the interviewer gets to see how I'd behave in a code review.
must_mention: ask for the case they have in mind

followups.q: Why not just stand firm?
followups.a: A live check is more persuasive and shows the code review behaviour they are hiring for.

traps: Changing a correct answer because the interviewer frowned.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview cheatsheet

q: Do you have any questions for me?
plain: Yes, always. Ask one or two specific questions: one about the technical work, one about how success is measured, ideally picking up something the interviewer said earlier. Done well, the question picks up something said earlier in the interview. Done badly: 'No, you covered everything.'
deep: The Handbook: candidates with no questions can seem uninterested; questions reveal what you care about. Good options: most costly early technical decision the team lives with; how a model change is evaluated before shipping; what success looks like in the first months; a result the team believed that did not hold. Avoid questions answered on the website; leave pay and logistics to the recruiter.
say: Yes, two. You mentioned earlier that retrieval quality is a big focus. How do you decide a retrieval change is actually better before it ships, and who decides when the eval set itself is wrong? And second, what's an early technical decision the team still lives with today? I ask that one because it tells me a lot about where the hard problems are. If there's time, I'd also love to hear what you'd want someone in this role to have solved in their first few months.

followups.q: What if they already answered your questions?
followups.a: Say so and ask a follow up on what they said, which shows you were listening.

traps: 'No, I think you covered everything.'

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: final questions to ask

q: Tell me about yourself.
plain: Give a 60 to 90 second pitch: where you are now, what you are good at, two short proofs chosen for this role, and why this role. Not a life history. Done well, it takes about a minute and ends on why this role. Done badly, it starts with high school and is still in 2023 at minute three.
deep: Elevator pitch structure from the Handbook: background, highlights with a number or challenge, why you fit. Rotate the two proofs by role (BEIR and EvidenceOps for retrieval; Dr. GRPO for post training; distributed ViT for infrastructure; JMA and ProProfs for analyst roles; handoff and the tool graph for agents). Keep personal contact details, work authorisation and salary out of the answer.
say: I'm finishing an MS in Applied Data Science at Syracuse. I build retrieval, evaluation and agent systems, and the part I'm best at is measuring where they break. For example, I replicated the BEIR retrieval benchmark on a laptop and traced the one number that didn't reproduce to a 100 token default that silently truncated every abstract. I'm also a research assistant on Gravity Spy, the NSF funded LIGO citizen science project, where I built the ingestion pipeline and a paired spectrogram model. I'm applying here because your team ships retrieval to people who act on the answers, and that's exactly the failure surface I like working on.

followups.q: What if they want more on a project?
followups.a: Go to that project's 60 second version.

followups.q: Should you mention grades or coursework?
followups.a: Only if the role asks for them; projects carry more signal.

traps: A year by year history.
Mentioning visa status or salary expectations here.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: self introduction

q: How do you practise explaining technical work?
plain: Daily short reps: answer cards out loud, record them, score against a checklist, and fix one thing each day. Weekly: a mock interview and explaining a project to someone non technical. Done well, practice is out loud, recorded and scored against a checklist. Done badly, practice is rereading notes silently, which builds recognition, not speech.
deep: Routine: 5 minutes of layered warm ups (10 and 30 second versions); 15 minutes of card drills recorded and scored against must mention items and traps; 5 minutes on one project's 60 second version plus two follow ups; 5 minutes reviewing one recording for the first sentence, filler count and where the thread was lost. Weekly mock with a person or an AI told to push follow ups, which the Handbook suggests; Feynman style explanation to a non technical friend. Amazon's guide suggests recording yourself or practising with a friend so STAR answers stay concise.
say: Every day I do about thirty minutes out loud, not in my head. I warm up by saying three concepts in ten seconds and then thirty. Then I answer five flashcards while recording on my phone, and score myself against each card's checklist of things I should have mentioned. I do one project story a day from memory, then two of its follow ups. Then I play one recording back and listen for whether my first sentence actually answered the question, and how many filler words I used. Once a week I do a mock with someone who keeps asking follow ups, and I explain a project to a non technical friend.

followups.q: Why record?
followups.a: What you hear on playback differs from how it felt; the recording shows what the interviewer heard.

traps: Practising silently by rereading notes.

source.title: Amazon interview guide

topic: Behavioural answers with STAR and CAR
q: What makes a strong answer to a 'tell me about a time' question?
plain: A short setup, most of the time on what you personally did and why, a result with a number and its limits, and what you learned. Open with a one line title so the interviewer knows which skill you are showing. Done well, the title alone tells the interviewer which skill is coming. Done badly, the story spends a minute on the company's history and ten seconds on what you did.
deep: STAR or CAR; Exponent puts most time on Action and wants quantified results; Amazon asks for 'I' statements and answers of typically 2 to 3 minutes; the Handbook adds Reflection as a seniority signal and recommends bullets over memorised scripts. interviewing.io: story selection matters more than delivery; a title that teases the challenge and evidence helps. Timing for 2 minutes: setup 20 s, action 70 s, result 20 s, learning 10 s. Actions should be decisions with alternatives considered.
say: A strong answer is mostly about what I did and why. I open with a one line title, like 'the time a default setting silently truncated every document', so they know what skill is coming. Then twenty seconds of context, then most of the time on my decisions: what I did, why, and what the alternative was, saying 'I' for my part and crediting the team once. The result has a number with its denominator and its caveat, and I finish with what I changed afterwards. Then I stop, because a two minute story will get twenty minutes of follow ups and those are where the real signal is.

followups.q: How long should it be?
followups.a: About two minutes; Amazon's guide says 2 to 3.

followups.q: What if I don't have a number?
followups.a: Give a concrete observable result and say honestly that it was not measured.

traps: Rushing to the result.
A story where everything went smoothly.

source.title: Amazon interview guide

topic: Behavioural answers with STAR and CAR
q: When would you use CAR instead of STAR?
plain: CAR (Context, Action, Result) merges the situation and task, which suits short answers and simple setups. STAR helps when the goal you were given differs from the situation, or when the loop expects that structure, as at Amazon. Done well, the format fits the time available and the action still gets most of it. Done badly, the answer recites the four STAR labels out loud like a form.
deep: STAR separates Situation from Task, useful when the task was assigned inside a messy context or when you set your own target (the Handbook notes 'Target' as a variant). CAR is leaner for phone screens or when context is one sentence. CARL adds Learning; STAR(R) adds Reflection. Either way the Action dominates. Choose by time available and the company's expectations; Amazon's guide names STAR explicitly.
say: I use CAR when the setup is simple or time is short, like a phone screen, because context, action and result keep it tight. STAR earns its extra part when the task was distinct from the situation, say the project was in chaos but my assignment was one narrow goal, or when I set the target myself. At Amazon I'd use STAR because it's what their guide asks for. In both, the action is most of the answer, and I add a closing line on what I learned, which some people call CARL. The format matters much less than picking the right story.
must_mention: STAR when the task differs from the situation

followups.q: Does format really matter?
followups.a: Less than story selection; interviewing.io's analysis of down leveled candidates found the mistakes were about story choice and content.

traps: Spending half the answer on the situation.

source.title: interviewing.io: stop memorizing STAR

q: How do you prepare stories for behavioural interviews?
plain: Build a story bank: 8 to 10 true stories written as bullet points, each mapped to the prompts it can answer, like conflict, failure, ambiguity or influence. The interviewing.io approach is to brainstorm many candidates, write down for each what made it hard and what evidence proves it, and delete any story missing either. One project can answer several prompts with different evidence; your JMA Wireless project covers both conflict and influence. Practise each story at 30 seconds and at 2 minutes, out loud. Done badly, you memorise scripts word for word and sound recited, or you arrive with three stories and stretch them to fit every question.
deep: Process (interviewing.io, Gilad Naor): brainstorm 20 to 30 candidate stories against the company's evaluation dimensions; for each, write what was hard (scope, ambiguity, coordination, time pressure) and the evidence (numbers, stakeholder seniority, before and after); delete stories lacking both; keep 6 to 10; give each a title that teases the challenge and evidence. The Tech Interview Handbook suggests anchoring on 3 to 5 large projects and preparing the big three: tell me about yourself, your favourite project, and a conflict. Map for this reader: conflict and influence (JMA), failure (EvidenceOps registry), ambiguity (Gravity Spy schemas), incomplete data (Dr. GRPO one seed), mistake caught (BEIR DPR), surprise (distributed ViT), teaching (TA), customer focus (ProProfs).
say: I build a bank of eight to ten true stories ahead of time, written as bullets, not scripts, and I map each one to the prompts it can answer. For every candidate story I write down two things: what made it genuinely hard, and what evidence proves the outcome, like numbers or who was involved. If a story is missing either, I drop it. One project can cover several prompts; my JMA Wireless project works for conflict and for influencing without authority, with different evidence for each. Then I practise each story out loud at thirty seconds for phone screens and two minutes for full rounds.
must_mention: what was hard and the evidence

followups.q: What if a question doesn't fit any story?
followups.a: Pick the closest story and say which part of it answers the question.

followups.q: How do you choose between two stories?
followups.a: The one with clearer difficulty and stronger evidence at the level you are interviewing for.

traps: Memorising scripts word for word.
Stories where everything went smoothly.

source.title: interviewing.io: stop memorizing STAR

q: Tell me about a time you failed.
plain: Use EvidenceOps: the retraction registry design caught none of the real retractions on a real slice of data, you found out why, fixed it, and changed how you test. This is a strong failure story because the failure was real, the cause was found, and the fix was measured. Done badly, a failure story is a disguised boast like 'I care too much about quality'.
deep: Title: 'the retraction registry that caught 0 of 3 on real data'. Context: registry built from retraction notices linking to targets; fixtures placed a notice next to its target. Action: parsed 5,000 real articles (no model involved), compared against PMC's own is_retracted flag, found all 11 notices pointed outside the slice. Result: notices only 0 of 3; merged the publisher flag as a second source, 3 of 3. Learning: synthetic fixtures can guarantee a metric (the leak of 0.000 on the four article synthetic corpus with the stub adapter was measured under conditions that guaranteed it); measure on real data early.
say: The time my retraction registry caught zero of three. In EvidenceOps I built the registry of retracted papers from the retraction notices themselves, and on my synthetic test corpus it worked perfectly. When I parsed 5,000 real articles, with no model involved, and compared against PMC's own retraction flag, the registry caught none of the three flagged articles. I dug in and found every one of the eleven notices pointed at an article outside the slice, which is structural: any filtered corpus splits notices from their targets. I added the publisher flag as a second source, which caught three of three. What I changed is that I now treat a perfect score on a fixture as suspicious.
must_mention: structural cause: filter splits notices from targets

followups.q: Why didn't tests catch it?
followups.a: The fixture placed the notice next to its target, so the case could not occur.

followups.q: What would you do differently?
followups.a: Run a small real slice before trusting any fixture metric.

traps: Picking a fake failure like 'I work too hard'.
Quoting the 0.000 leak without its synthetic caveat.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: behavioral interview rubrics

q: Tell me about a time you had to influence people you had no authority over.
plain: Use JMA Wireless: as a student project lead on a client engagement, you used shared definitions and data to show the constraint was upstream material flow, not the equipment people suspected. The numbers did the persuading, which is the point of an influence story. Done badly, the story says 'I convinced them' with no evidence of how.
deep: Title: 'the machine that ran 97 percent of the time and missed plan by half'. Context: client DMAIC engagement, four person student team, sponsor the SVP of Global Operations; functions defined KPIs differently. Actions: definition interviews across manufacturing, quality and supervision; a sponsor approved definitions document for five KPIs; flattened the automated cell's JSON (31 GB raw) to under 5 MB so it could be measured; showed 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of weekly target, which implies input limited; picked three fixes from six with a Pugh matrix. Result: 2 week standup pilot cut median red to owner acting from about 4 hours to about 25 minutes. Caveat: short pilot; value of about USD 355,000 a year is projected pending Finance.
say: At JMA Wireless I led a four person student team on a client project, so I had no authority over anyone on the floor. Everyone suspected the automated cell's equipment. I first got the functions to agree on what Uptime and Schedule Attainment meant, through interviews and a definitions document the sponsor signed. Then I made the cell measurable by flattening its nested JSON from over 31 gigabytes to under 5 megabytes. Measured the same way, it ran 97.3 percent of the time but hit only 46.3 percent of its weekly target, which means it was starved upstream. The data did the persuading; a two week pilot cut the time from a red KPI to an owner acting from about four hours to about twenty five minutes.
must_mention: 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of target

followups.q: How did you handle people who still blamed the machine?
followups.a: Put both numbers side by side; a machine that runs almost all the time cannot be the reason it misses plan by half.

followups.q: Was the value realised?
followups.a: No, about USD 355,000 a year is a projection resting on written assumptions that JMA Finance still has to confirm.

traps: Claiming the projected value as realised savings.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: behavioral interview rubrics

q: Tell me about a time you faced ambiguity.
plain: Use Gravity Spy: you had to build a pipeline over data from several project iterations whose metadata formats were not documented, and you reconciled them before anything else could work. The ambiguity was concrete and the actions made it smaller. Done badly, an ambiguity story is 'requirements kept changing and I adapted' with no specifics.
deep: Context: Gravity Spy 2.0, NSF funded LIGO citizen science; 276,000 plus volunteer classifications over 23 months. Ambiguity: five undocumented subject metadata schemas from different project iterations, covering 25,104 glitch subjects and 8,293 auxiliary channels; science team accounts mixed into volunteers. Actions: reconciled schemas, filtered about 38 science team accounts, wrote separate outputs including a file for subjects missing GPS metadata rather than dropping them silently. Result: a subject level flat file, a GPS by channel pivot over 455 subsystems, and a model at 0.89 validation AUC on 2,000 held out subjects.
say: On Gravity Spy, the LIGO citizen science project, I had to ingest more than 276,000 volunteer classifications collected over 23 months, and the subject metadata came in five different schemas from earlier iterations of the project, none of them documented. Nobody could tell me which fields meant the same thing. I worked it out from the data itself, reconciled the five schemas across 25,104 glitch subjects, and filtered out about 38 science team accounts so they didn't count as volunteers. Where I couldn't resolve something, like subjects missing GPS times, I wrote them to a separate file instead of dropping them, so the ambiguity stayed visible for the science team.
must_mention: result usable by the science team

followups.q: How did you validate the reconciliation?
followups.a: Have your concrete checks ready, such as counts per iteration and spot checks against the project site.

traps: Describing ambiguity as 'requirements changed' with no specifics.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: behavioral interview rubrics

q: Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete data.
plain: Use Dr. GRPO: with only one training seed, you chose to publish the result with intervals and word the verdict carefully, rather than claim the paper was wrong or spend more compute first. The decision was about what to claim, which is a real decision with incomplete data. Done badly, the story hides the uncertainty and claims more than the data supports.
deep: Context: replication of Liu and colleagues 2025 on Qwen2.5-1.5B; one seed (paper used three); each extra seed about 4.4 GPU hours. Decision: stop at seed 0, publish paired bootstrap intervals, verdict 'not reproduced here', not 'refuted'. Evidence: accuracy 51.6 against 51.2 percent on MATH500, paired plus 0.4 points [minus 3.4, plus 4.0]; wrong answers 680 against 545 tokens. Trade off: intervals capture variation over problems and steps, not seeds, and identical runs drift because fp16 backward passes are not bit reproducible.
say: In my Dr. GRPO replication I had one seed where the paper had three, and each extra seed would cost about four and a half GPU hours. The result was surprising: accuracy held, 51.6 against 51.2 percent on MATH500, but both length claims came out reversed. I had to decide what to claim. I chose to publish with paired bootstrap intervals and to word it as 'not reproduced here' rather than 'refuted', because the intervals cover variation across problems and steps, not across seeds, and identical runs drift apart on GPUs. The data was incomplete, so I made the claim match the data, and named the next two seeds as the first follow up.

followups.q: Would you decide the same way at work?
followups.a: Yes, when a decision is reversible I ship the honest partial result and the plan to complete it.

traps: Overclaiming the paper is wrong.

q: Tell me about a time you caught a mistake that others would have missed.
plain: Use BEIR: one number was far below the paper, you found the cause was a hidden 100 token limit in a library default, and you proved it with a sweep that matched the paper exactly. The catch came from noticing a number that did not make sense and testing a specific hypothesis. Done badly, the story says 'I found a bug' with no account of how you found it.
deep: Title: 'the default that cut every abstract to 100 tokens'. Context: BEIR replication; TAS-B had reproduced exactly, so the loader and metrics were fine. Observation: DPR on SciFact 0.260 against published 0.318. The tell: title only 0.261 equals title plus text 0.260, so the body contributed nothing. Cause: sentence-transformers port of DPR's context encoder ships max_seq_length = 100. Fix: sweep 100, 256, 350, 512; at 512 nDCG@10 0.318 and Recall@100 0.727 matched published. Why others would miss it: NFCorpus, with 38.2 judged documents per query against 1.1, reproduced either way.
say: In my BEIR replication, DPR on SciFact scored 0.260 against a published 0.318. Since TAS-B had matched exactly, I knew the loader and metrics were fine, so it had to be something about how DPR sees documents. The tell was that searching with titles only scored the same as titles plus full text, which only happens if the text is being thrown away. The sentence-transformers port of DPR's encoder ships with a 100 token limit and silently truncates. I swept the limit, and at 512 it matched the paper exactly. It would have been easy to miss, because the other dataset reproduced either way; it has many judged documents per query and absorbs the damage.
must_mention: TAS-B exact ruled out the pipeline
title only equals title plus text

followups.q: How would you catch this class of bug in production?
followups.a: Check the embedder's configured limit against the chunk length distribution automatically.

traps: Saying 'I tuned it until it matched'.

q: Tell me about a time a result surprised you.
plain: Use the distributed ViT project: making each GPU faster with fp16 made two GPU scaling much worse, because the bottleneck moved to the CPU decoding images. The surprise is followed by an experiment that isolated the cause. Done badly, a surprise story ends at 'and that was unexpected'.
deep: Title: 'the speedup that vanished when the GPUs got faster'. On 2 T4s: fp32 1,853 to 3,637 img/s (98 percent efficiency); fp16 3,810 to 4,376 (57 percent). Hypotheses: nccl all reduce versus input pipeline. Isolation: synthetic tensors from memory, no decode or augmentation, restored 1.92 times at 96 percent, so the collective was innocent; Kaggle's 4 vCPUs could not feed the second GPU. A second surprise: on the M5, 1 to 4 gloo ranks raised throughput from 552 to 879 img/s, the opposite of the predicted slowdown, so the prediction was deleted.
say: On my distributed ViT project, two T4 GPUs scaled at 98 percent efficiency in fp32, which was great. Then I turned on fp16, each GPU got about twice as fast, and two GPU efficiency fell to 57 percent. I expected the all reduce to be the problem, but instead of tweaking dataloader workers and guessing, I added a synthetic input mode that feeds tensors from memory with no image decoding at all. That restored 96 percent. So the communication was innocent; Kaggle's four CPUs couldn't decode images fast enough to feed the second GPU. The lesson was that speeding up one layer just moves the bottleneck, so I measure the whole pipeline.
must_mention: bottleneck moved to the host CPUs

followups.q: What would you change?
followups.a: Pre decoded tensors or GPU side augmentation to feed the faster GPUs.

traps: Telling a surprise with no investigation.

q: Tell me about a disagreement or conflict at work.
plain: Use JMA Wireless: different functions meant different things by the same KPIs, so comparisons went in circles until you ran definition interviews and got one sponsor approved definition per KPI. This frames conflict honestly as a disagreement about definitions. Done badly, a conflict story blames a colleague or invents drama you cannot back up when asked for detail.
deep: Context: manufacturing, quality and production supervision each used Uptime and Schedule Attainment differently, so the manual line and automated cell could not be compared. Action: definition interviews with each function; a definitions document fixing one formula and one target for five KPIs (Parts per Labor Hour, Uptime, First Time Throughput, Schedule Attainment, a Culture and Engagement index); sponsor approval. Result: both lines measured the same way, which surfaced the input limited cell. Frame it honestly as a conflict of definitions, not personalities, and only add interpersonal detail you can stand behind.
say: At JMA Wireless the conflict was about definitions, which is more common than personality clashes. Manufacturing, quality and supervision each meant something different by Uptime and Schedule Attainment, so every comparison between the manual line and the automated cell turned into an argument about numbers. I interviewed each function separately to understand why their definition made sense for their job, then wrote one document fixing a single formula and target for five KPIs and got the sponsor to approve it. Once everyone measured the same way, the argument stopped and the data showed the real constraint was upstream material flow. I learned to settle definitions before debating results.
must_mention: one formula and target per KPI

followups.q: What if a function refused the definition?
followups.a: Escalate to the sponsor with both definitions and what each would mean for the decision.

traps: Inventing interpersonal drama you cannot back up.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: behavioral interview rubrics

topic: How to tell a project story
q: Walk me through a project you're proud of.
plain: Pick the project that fits the role and give its 60 second version: the problem, what you built, the result with its caveat, and a hook for a follow up. Then stop and let them choose where to dig. Done well, you stop after the minute and let them choose where to dig. Done badly, you narrate the tech stack file by file.
deep: Five layers per project: 15 s, 60 s, 3 min deep dive (problem, why it matters, what I built, hardest decision and trade off, result with honest caveats, next), five prepared follow ups, owned weak spots. Rules: numbers with denominators and provenance; caveats in the same sentence; lead with the surprise. The Handbook suggests choosing at the intersection of impact, scope and personal involvement.
say: I'd pick the one that fits the role, and I give it in about a minute: the problem, what I built, the result with its caveat, and the surprising part. For a retrieval role that's my BEIR replication. I rebuilt BEIR's claim that BM25 beats dense retrievers out of domain, on SciFact and NFCorpus. It held for the paper's models, it didn't survive a 2023 embedder, and the one number that missed traced to a 100 token default silently truncating documents. Then I stop, because the interviewer can choose whether to go into the bug, the BM25 implementation, or what I'd change.

followups.q: How do you pick?
followups.a: Impact, scope and how much of it was yours, matched to the role.

traps: Describing the tech stack instead of the problem and the finding.

source.title: Tech Interview Handbook: behavioral interviews

topic: How to tell a project story
q: What's the weakest part of that project?
plain: Name the real weak spot before they find it, explain why it exists, and say what would fix it. Owning a limitation shows judgement. Done well, the weakness is real and comes with its fix. Done badly, the weakness is 'I was too thorough'.
deep: Pattern: name it, why it exists, what it bounds, the fix and its cost. Example for Dr. GRPO: one seed; intervals capture problems and steps, not seeds; verdict worded as not reproduced here; seeds 1 and 2 at about 4.4 GPU hours each are next. For EvidenceOps: no real model yet; metrics on a four article synthetic corpus with a stub adapter show plumbing only. Avoid fake weaknesses.
say: For my Dr. GRPO replication, it's that I ran one seed. The paper used three. My bootstrap intervals cover variation across problems and training steps, but not across seeds, and two identical runs on GPUs drift apart after the first update. So I deliberately call the length result 'not reproduced here' rather than 'refuted'. The fix is cheap and known: seeds one and two cost about four and a half GPU hours each and they're the first thing I'd run. I'd rather tell you that up front than have it come out in the fifth follow up.

followups.q: Why volunteer weaknesses?
followups.a: Research interviewers will find them anyway; naming them first shows you know the limits of your evidence.

traps: Naming a weakness that is really a strength.

q: Give me EvidenceOps in one sentence.
plain: The 15 second version is: EvidenceOps is a retrieval and answer system over PubMed Central open access papers that treats retraction status as a correctness constraint, so if the best evidence has been withdrawn it refuses and says so instead of citing it fluently. That single line carries the problem (retracted papers are often the most relevant), the design choice (a constraint, not a ranking signal) and the behaviour (refuse and explain). Done well, it stops there and lets the interviewer pick a direction. Done badly, it lists six services and four storage planes before the point appears.
deep: Use this as the opener when time is short or as the first layer of the 60 second version. Hooks it plants: why retraction is not a ranking feature (ADR 0001), why query time resolution (ADR 0003), and how it is evaluated (the synthetic corpus and stub caveat). Never attach a metric to the 15 second version, because any EvidenceOps metric needs its caveat in the same sentence.
say: EvidenceOps is a retrieval and answer system over PubMed Central open access papers that treats retraction as a correctness constraint rather than a ranking signal. The reason is that the retracted paper is often the most relevant document for the question, so a normal RAG system will cite it fluently and correctly and still be wrong in a way the reader can't detect. So when the best evidence has been withdrawn, it refuses and says which notice withdrew it. I usually stop there and let the interviewer choose whether to go into the trust design, the guardrails or how I evaluated it.
must_mention: retracted paper is often most relevant

followups.q: Why not just rank retracted papers lower?
followups.a: Because the relevance is real; only a hard constraint keeps them out of the answer.

traps: Adding a metric without its synthetic corpus and stub caveat.

q: Walk me through EvidenceOps.
plain: A question answering system over PubMed Central papers that treats retraction status as a hard correctness rule. Its evaluation numbers come from a four article synthetic corpus with a deterministic stub adapter, so they show the plumbing works, not model quality. Think of a librarian who checks the withdrawal list before handing you a paper. On the synthetic fixture with the stub adapter, the registry turns a fluent answer built on a retracted biomarker paper into a block that names the retraction notice.
deep: Six services (ingest, retrieval, guard, gateway, evalsvc, agent) and four storage planes (DuckDB and dbt metadata, vectors, BM25 on the same chunk ids, a JSONL trust registry). Request path: hybrid retrieval with RRF and reranking, live trust resolution, a refusal check before any model call, gateway routing, synthesis with a chunk id per sentence, citation verification banded by lexical overlap, and a guard that collapses findings to approve, warn, rewrite, review or block. Domain core: stdlib, numpy, pyyaml. Real, reproducible facts: 107 tests per the README; statement coverage over services from 75 to 84 percent. Real slice: 5,000 articles parsed with no model, 6 parser bugs, registry recall 0 of 3 from notices, 3 of 3 with PMC's flag.
say: EvidenceOps answers questions over PubMed Central open access papers, built on one observation: an answer that cites a retracted paper is worse than a refusal, because it's fluent, correctly sourced and wrong. So retraction is a correctness constraint with its own registry, looked up at query time, so a retraction published tonight applies to the next query without reindexing. Nine deterministic guardrails run before any model call. Its evaluation numbers come from a four article synthetic corpus with a deterministic stub, so they show plumbing, not quality; what's solid is 107 tests and coverage up from 75 to 84 percent. On 5,000 real articles, parsed with no model, my notice based registry caught 0 of 3 retractions, which changed the design.
must_mention: synthetic corpus and stub caveat with every metric
0 of 3 on 5,000 real articles, then 3 of 3

followups.q: Is any of it measured with a real model?
followups.a: No. The Ollama path has not been run; bge-small was swapped in once and the stub synthesiser stayed.

followups.q: What did the real data change?
followups.a: The registry now merges PMC's own retraction flag as a second source, because filtered corpora split notices from their targets.

traps: Quoting the 0.857 pass rate or the 0.000 leak without the synthetic corpus and stub caveat.
Linking a public repository; there is none.

q: Take me through EvidenceOps in depth.
plain: The deep dive follows six beats: the problem, why it matters, what you built, the hardest decision with its trade off, the result with honest caveats, and what you would do next. For EvidenceOps the hardest decision is resolving trust at query time and keeping retracted chunks retrievable so the system can explain a refusal. The result section must keep every number tied to its source: stub runs on a four article synthetic corpus show the plumbing, while the 5,000 article real parse showed the registry design failing and being fixed. Done well, it takes about three minutes and leaves hooks for follow ups. Done badly, it becomes a tour of the folder structure.
deep: Problem: relevance work assumes every indexed document is citable; retracted papers break that, and often are the most relevant. Why: a fluent, correctly cited answer on withdrawn evidence is undetectable to the reader; the system also refuses individualised medical advice on request and response.
