Built: ingest, retrieval (dense plus BM25, RRF, rerank), guard (nine detectors, citation verification, policy), gateway, evalsvc, agent; four planes (DuckDB and dbt, vectors, BM25, JSONL trust registry); core on stdlib, numpy, pyyaml. Hardest decision: query time trust (ADR 0003), costs a serving path lookup and storage on uncitable chunks. Result: on the four article synthetic fixture with the stub adapter, the demo blocks at confidence 0.0573 although retrieval scored 0.5933 and citation support 1.0, and the golden set passes 0.857 with leak 0.000 under conditions that guaranteed it; on 5,000 real articles (no model) six parser bugs and registry recall 0 of 3, fixed to 3 of 3. Next: real model behind the gateway, 120 case golden set, 50 human labels, dense only against hybrid plus rerank ablation.
say: The problem is that retrieval work assumes every document in the index is citable, and retracted papers break that. I built six services: ingest, hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, a guard with nine deterministic detectors and citation checks and three supporting services, on a core with no framework dependencies. The hardest decision was resolving trust at query time and keeping retracted chunks retrievable, so the guard can say the best evidence was withdrawn; the cost is a lookup per query. On a four article synthetic corpus with a stub adapter it blocks the retracted case correctly, which proves plumbing only. Real data was humbling: on 5,000 articles the registry caught 0 of 3 retractions until I added PMC's flag. Next is a real model and a bigger eval set.
must_mention: query time trust and retrievable retracted chunks
stub on synthetic corpus proves plumbing only
0 of 3 then 3 of 3 on real data

followups.q: What would you cut first?
followups.a: The two labs folders, which are READMEs rather than code; the retrieval, guard and evaluation path is the thesis and stays.

traps: Spending the three minutes on architecture and none on the result and caveats.

q: Why resolve retraction status at query time instead of filtering at index time?
plain: Because papers get retracted after they are indexed. If the status lives in the index, a retraction does nothing until someone reindexes. Looking it up on every query makes it take effect immediately. It is like checking a recall list at the checkout instead of only when stock arrives.
deep: ADR 0003: the payload carries index time status only as a hint; `RetrievalEngine._apply_live_trust` reads the registry on every retrieval. Failure mode avoided: an article indexed in good standing and retracted eighteen months later still says ok. Second half: retracted chunks stay retrievable so the guard can say the best evidence was withdrawn instead of silently serving the second best chunk with equal confidence. Costs: a registry lookup on the serving path (thousands of rows, in memory) and storage spent on chunks that will never be citable.
say: Because retraction happens after indexing, often years after publication. If I write trust status into the vector payload, an article indexed in good standing and retracted eighteen months later still says 'ok' until someone rebuilds the index, and the system serves withdrawn evidence with a perfect looking citation. So the payload value is only a hint, and the authoritative lookup happens on every retrieval; a retraction recorded tonight applies at the next query. I also keep retracted chunks retrievable, so the guard can say 'the best evidence was withdrawn' rather than quietly using the second best chunk. The costs are a lookup on the serving path, which is tiny, and storage on chunks that can never be cited.
must_mention: keep retracted chunks retrievable to explain refusals
costs: serving path dependency and storage

followups.q: What if the registry service is down?
followups.a: Fail closed for citation: refuse rather than serve unverified evidence, and alert.

followups.q: How big is the registry?
followups.a: Thousands of rows per the ADR, so it fits in memory.

traps: Saying a reranker could handle retractions.

q: Your EvidenceOps metrics come from a stub. What do they actually show?
plain: They show the pipeline wiring is correct: the right source is retrieved, citations attach to the right chunks, retracted evidence is blocked and the release gates fire. They say nothing about answer quality from a real model. A stub is a stand in that always behaves the same way, which is good for testing wiring and useless for judging quality. The numbers are honest only with that label attached.
deep: Every reported run records adapter and embedder names so a stub run cannot be mistaken for a model run. On the four article synthetic fixture with the stub adapter: golden pass rate 0.857 over 14 cases, retracted evidence leak 0.000 (measured under conditions that guaranteed it), hedging appropriateness 0.25 (measuring the stub). The bge-small swap with the same stub synthesiser raised pass rate to 0.929 while rerank scores stayed byte identical and g012 passed with an unresponsive answer, which showed every metric was about provenance. A rank aware metric was then added: answer chunk MRR 0.8370 to 0.9259 when headings were indexed, on the same synthetic fixture with the stub.
say: They show the wiring, not the intelligence. On a four article synthetic corpus with a deterministic stub adapter, the pipeline retrieves the right source, binds citations to the right chunks, blocks the retracted paper and fires its release gates. That's what the 0.857 pass rate on 14 cases means, under that caveat. The most useful thing the stub runs taught me was the harness's own blind spot: when I swapped in a real embedder, pass rate went up while the answer to one question didn't address it at all, because every metric was about provenance. So I added a metric that sees the rank of the answering chunk. Model quality needs a real model, which is the next step.
must_mention: four article synthetic corpus, stub adapter
harness blind spot: provenance, not responsiveness

followups.q: Then why report them at all?
followups.a: Because they are regression tests for the plumbing, and the README labels them so nobody mistakes them for model results.

traps: Calling 0.857 an accuracy.

q: What broke when EvidenceOps first met real data?
plain: Six bugs the synthetic test files had hidden, including one where every real article lost its ID without any error, and a structural problem where the retraction registry missed every real retraction in the sample. For example, real PMC files label the article id differently from the test files, so every real article came out with an empty id and nothing raised an error. The project keeps this fix list because each bug is invisible until real data arrives.
deep: 5,000 commercial use articles from the PMC S3 bucket, parsed with no model. Fix list: default prefix pointed at a zero byte marker (fetch reported success with nothing); empty prefix fell back to default because empty string is falsy; version suffix kept on ids; parser read pub-id-type pmc while real files use pmcid, so every live article parsed to an empty id silently; OCR bodies in preformat discarded (170 of 5,000); notices harvested targets from their reference lists, which would fabricate retractions. Registry: 11 notices all pointing outside the slice, recall 0 of 3; with PMC flags 3 of 3.
say: Six things, all invisible on the four synthetic test files with a green suite. The worst was quiet: my parser read the PMC id from an attribute value that real files don't use, so every live article came out with an empty id, nothing raised, and every trust lookup downstream would have failed open. Another bug went the dangerous other way: notices were picking up targets from their reference lists, which would mark sound papers as retracted. And structurally, all eleven notices in the 5,000 article slice pointed outside it, so the registry caught zero of three real retractions until I added PMC's own flag. That fix list is the most valuable output of the project.

followups.q: Which bug was worse?
followups.a: The fabricated retraction, because it blocks sound evidence and looks exactly like the system working.

traps: Widening exception handling to hide parse failures.

q: How does EvidenceOps check that a citation actually supports a claim, without calling a judge on every one?
plain: It bands citations by word overlap between the claim and the cited chunk. Below 0.25 the citation is rejected for free, above 0.80 it is accepted for free, and only the uncertain middle goes to a paid model judge. That puts cheap deterministic checks in front of expensive ones. On the synthetic fixture with the stub adapter, 1 of 6 citations needed the judge, but that number means little because the stub copies text almost verbatim. The real share has to be measured with a real model.
deep: Layering: nine deterministic detectors run first (unknown citation, trust status, uncited claim, licence violation, PII, causal overreach, clinical directive, absolute claim, advice seeking request), free and stable between runs. Citation verification: lexical overlap prefilter with a floor of 0.25 (reject) and a ceiling of 0.80 (accept); the middle goes to the judge. Fixture result (stub, four article synthetic corpus): 6 citations, 0 rejected, 5 accepted without a judge, 1 to the judge (17 percent). Outcomes are graded (approve, approve with warning, rewrite, human review, block); rewrite repairs causal overreach, for example turning 'causes' into 'is associated with' on observational evidence.
say: With two free thresholds around a paid judge. The verifier measures word overlap between the claim and the chunk it cites. Below 0.25 the citation is rejected with no model call, above 0.80 it's accepted with no model call, and only the ambiguous middle reaches the judge. Before that, nine deterministic detectors run, things like an uncited claim or causal language on observational evidence, which are free and never disagree with themselves. On the synthetic fixture with the stub adapter, one of six citations needed the judge, but the stub copies text almost verbatim, so that share is meaningless until a real model writes the answers.

followups.q: What is the risk of the ceiling?
followups.a: High overlap with the opposite conclusion, the calibration trap c006, would be auto accepted; that is why the judge needs calibration.

traps: Claiming the 17 percent judge share as a cost saving result.

q: Why did you build EvidenceOps without LangGraph or Pydantic in the core?
plain: The domain core depends only on the Python standard library, numpy and pyyaml, so the whole pipeline, including citation checks and the eval harness, runs in CI in under a minute with no network, GPU or model download. Every external system sits behind an interface with a free default, such as a hashing embedder or an in memory vector store, and swapping to production backends is a configuration change. The agent's state machine is written by hand with node names that map one to one onto LangGraph. The cost is hand written validation and no built in streaming, checkpointing or retries. It is a deliberate trade recorded in ADRs 0002 and 0004.
deep: ADR 0002: frameworks only at the HTTP edge (the api.py modules); protocols with zero cost defaults (HashingEmbedder, InMemoryVectorStore, FakeAdapter) and production implementations (SentenceTransformerEmbedder with bge-small, QdrantVectorStore int8, OllamaAdapter). Consequence noted in the ADR: the tool argument validator is hand written, including the case where a boolean satisfies an integer parameter because bool subclasses int. ADR 0004: states INTAKE, PLAN, PERMISSION_CHECK, AWAITING_APPROVAL, EXECUTE, REFLECT, RESPOND, FAILED; planner output is untrusted input, validated against tool schema, role and rate limit; high risk tools pause with a dry run.
say: Two reasons: testability and legibility. The core only depends on the standard library, numpy and pyyaml, so CI runs the real pipeline, retrieval, citation checks and the eval harness, in under a minute with no network or GPU. Every external system sits behind an interface with a free default, and switching to bge-small or Qdrant is a change to the environment file. The agent's state machine maps one to one onto LangGraph's node names, so porting is mechanical. The costs are real: I wrote validation Pydantic would give me, including catching that a boolean passes as an integer in Python, and I don't get streaming, checkpointing or retries for free.
must_mention: CI under a minute, no network
costs: hand validation, no streaming or checkpoints

followups.q: Would you keep it that way in production?
followups.a: The core yes; at the edge I would adopt a framework for streaming, retries and persistence.

traps: Saying frameworks are bad in general.

q: How do you know your LLM judge in EvidenceOps is any good?
plain: You compare the judge against labels a person wrote and report agreement corrected for chance (Cohen's kappa) and the direction of its errors. For EvidenceOps that set is only 8 hand labels with the stub judge, which is enough to spot a bad judge, not to certify a good one. Kappa corrects for agreement you would get by chance. A judge that always says 'supported' would look 62.5 percent accurate on this set and still have a kappa of zero.
deep: Calibration on 8 hand labelled claim and evidence pairs, stub judge: agreement 0.625, kappa 0.25 (fair), bias too generous, 3 false positives, 0 false negatives. The misses are deliberate traps: same topic opposite conclusion, fact absent from the cited span, causal claim on observational evidence with high lexical overlap. Kappa $= (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)$; reporting it rather than raw agreement exposes a judge that always says supported (0.625 agreement here, kappa 0). Probe to prepare: with binary labels, 5 supported of 8, 3 false positives and 0 false negatives describes the always supported judge, whose kappa is 0, so check the label coding before quoting 0.25. Target: 50 or more labels written by a person.
say: I measure it against labels I wrote myself and report kappa, not raw agreement. In EvidenceOps the calibration set is only eight hand labelled pairs, scored against the stub judge: agreement 0.625, kappa 0.25, too generous, three false positives and no false negatives. The misses are traps I wrote on purpose, like a claim with the opposite conclusion on the same topic, or a causal claim on observational evidence with high word overlap. Kappa matters because a judge that always says 'supported' would also score 0.625 here. Eight labels can catch a bad judge but can't certify a good one, so the plan is fifty labels and a real model as judge.

followups.q: Why must a person label them?
followups.a: A model labelled calibration set measures agreement between models, not correctness.

followups.q: What's the formula?
followups.a: Observed agreement minus chance agreement, over one minus chance agreement.

traps: Reporting raw agreement only.
Quoting kappa 0.25 without knowing how it follows from the confusion matrix.

q: Is any of EvidenceOps measured with a real language model?
plain: No, and you should say so before you are asked. Every evaluation number comes from a four article synthetic corpus and a deterministic stub adapter, which tests the wiring, not answer quality. One real component has been run: the bge-small embedder was swapped in, with the stub synthesiser unchanged. The real data work is the 5,000 article parse, which involved no model. Owning this well means naming it, saying what is real instead, and naming the next step.
deep: Status from the results file: Ollama is not installed on the build machine, so the LLM half has not been run; hedging appropriateness sits at 0.25 because it measures the stub; golden cases g012 and g014 fail because the stub's lexical overlap floor refuses despite correct retrieval, and the threshold was deliberately not lowered. The bge-small swap (same stub) moved pass rate from 0.857 to 0.929, explained entirely by the stub's retrieval floor, while the lexical reranker produced byte identical scores. Real, reproducible facts: 107 tests per the README, statement coverage 75 to 84 percent; the 5,000 article parse with its fix list.
say: Not yet, and I'd rather say that first. Every evaluation number comes from a four article synthetic corpus and a deterministic stub adapter, so it shows the pipeline is wired correctly, not that the answers are good. I did swap in a real embedder, bge-small, while keeping the stub synthesiser, and that taught me the harness couldn't see whether an answer actually addressed the question. What is real is the 5,000 article parse, which needed no model and found six bugs, plus 107 tests and coverage up from 75 to 84 percent. The next step is putting a local model behind the gateway and rerunning the same golden set.
must_mention: four article synthetic corpus, stub adapter
what is real: parse, tests, coverage
next: local model, same golden set

followups.q: Why not just lower the stub's threshold to pass g012?
followups.a: Lowering a threshold to turn a case green destroys the measurement; the failure is documented instead.

traps: Letting the interviewer discover it in the fifth follow up.

q: What numbers in EvidenceOps would you be careful quoting?
plain: Several numbers have small denominators or come with conditions that guaranteed them. The 0.000 retracted evidence leak was measured on a synthetic fixture that placed the notice next to its target. The 100 percent notice link rate rests on 11 notices, 10 of them corrections against one retraction. The calibration kappa of 0.25 rests on 8 labels and is worth checking against the confusion matrix before quoting. And the test count differs between the README and an earlier section of the results file, so quote what you just ran.
deep: Details: leak 0.000 (four article synthetic fixture, stub adapter; the results file says it was measured under conditions that guaranteed it). Link rate 11 of 11 structured (real slice; n too small to retire the regex fallback). Judge: 8 labels, agreement 0.625, kappa 0.25, 3 false positives, 0 false negatives; with binary labels and 5 supported, 3 false positives and 0 false negatives would be the always supported judge, kappa 0, so verify the coding. Tests: README 107 (86 plus 21); results file section 1 lists 68 passed and 2 skipped bare, 89 with extras. Capacity: 4.77 GB int8 against 15.50 GB float32 for 10M chunks is a computed estimate, not a measurement.
say: Four of them. The zero retracted evidence leak was measured on a synthetic fixture that placed each retraction notice right next to its target, so it couldn't fail; real data showed the opposite. The 100 percent notice link rate rests on eleven notices, ten of them corrections against a single retraction. The judge's kappa of 0.25 is on eight labels, and I'd check it against the confusion matrix before quoting, because three false positives and no false negatives on binary labels would give a kappa of zero. And the README and an older section of the results file list different test counts, so I quote whatever the suite printed when I last ran it.
must_mention: kappa on 8 labels, check the matrix

followups.q: Why volunteer this?
followups.a: Because research interviewers check denominators, and finding these yourself is the evidence of rigour.

traps: Quoting the leak as proof that retraction handling works.

q: Give me the BEIR replication in one sentence.
plain: The 15 second version is: I reproduced BEIR's claim that BM25 beats dense retrievers out of domain, on SciFact and NFCorpus on one laptop; it held for the paper's models, did not survive a 2023 embedder, and the one cell that missed traced to a 100 token default. Each clause is a hook: the claim, the extension, and the bug. Done well, the interviewer picks one hook to pull. Done badly, it opens with the hardware and the libraries.
deep: Hooks and their follow ups: the claim (what nDCG@10 measures, counts matching the paper); the extension (bge-small-en-v1.5 at 0.713 and 0.343, labelled not in the paper); the bug (DPR 0.260 against 0.318, max_seq_length 100, fixed at 512). Keep 'extension' and 'reproduction' separate in speech, exactly as the README labels them.
say: I reproduced the central claim of the BEIR benchmark, that BM25 beats dense retrievers when you move them to a new domain, on its two scientific datasets that fit on a laptop. The claim held for the models the paper tested. It didn't survive a 2023 embedder, bge-small, which I label as an extension rather than a reproduction. And the one cell that didn't match the paper traced to a library default that silently cut every document to 100 tokens. Each of those three is a thread I'm happy to pull, but the truncation bug is usually the most interesting one.
must_mention: BM25 against dense, out of domain

followups.q: Which thread is most interesting?
followups.a: The truncation bug, because the same failure exists in any RAG system with long chunks.

traps: Calling the extension a reproduction.

q: Walk me through the BEIR replication.
plain: A laptop scale rebuild of the BEIR benchmark's claim that keyword search beats neural retrievers on unfamiliar domains, on two scientific datasets. It held for the paper's models, a 2023 model beat it, and the one cell that missed traced to a hidden 100 token limit. nDCG@10 scores how well the top ten results are ordered, where 1 is perfect. The surprising cell was DPR scoring 0.260 on SciFact against a published 0.318.
deep: Official BEIR data; counts match the paper (SciFact 5,183 and 300; NFCorpus 3,633 and 323); pytrec_eval metrics; BM25 in Python with k1 0.9, b 0.4, Porter, Lucene stopwords; per checkpoint similarity. nDCG@10 reproduced: BM25 0.677 and 0.320 (published 0.665 and 0.325), TAS-B 0.643 and 0.319 exact, DPR 0.318 and 0.188 after fixing truncation; bge-small 0.713 and 0.343 and hybrid RRF 0.687 and 0.341, both labelled not in the paper. DPR sweep: 0.276 at 100 tokens to 0.318 at 512 with title [SEP] text encoding.
say: I rebuilt the central claim of BEIR, that dense retrievers trained on MS MARCO lose to BM25 on new domains, on its two scientific datasets that fit a laptop, SciFact and NFCorpus. q: Why does the similarity function matter when you evaluate a dense retriever?
plain: Each dense model is trained to compare queries and documents with one particular scoring function, and using a different one changes the ranking. TAS-B and DPR were trained for dot product, so scoring them with cosine throws away the vector length the model learned to use. bge models expect cosine similarity plus an instruction prefix on the query. The BEIR README calls getting this wrong the easiest way to manufacture a fake negative result about dense retrieval. Done well, you state the scoring rule per checkpoint before reporting any number.
deep: Dot product $q^\top d = \lVert q\rVert \lVert d\rVert \cos\theta$ keeps magnitude; cosine normalises it away. A model trained with dot product can encode confidence or document salience in the norm, so cosine changes the order. In the replication: TAS-B and DPR scored with dot product, bge-small-en-v1.5 with cosine and its retrieval instruction on the query side, matching each checkpoint's training. Related deployment trap: vector databases default to a metric (often cosine), so the index metric must match the model.
say: Because each model was trained to score with one function, and the ranking changes if you use another. Dot product keeps the vector's length, cosine throws it away, and a model trained with dot product can store useful signal in that length. So in my BEIR replication I scored TAS-B and DPR with dot product, and bge-small with cosine plus its query instruction, matching how each checkpoint was trained. Getting this wrong is the easiest way to make dense retrieval look worse than it is. It matters in production too, because a vector database's default metric has to match the model.
must_mention: each checkpoint trained with one scoring rule
index metric must match the model

followups.q: What happens if you normalise the vectors?
followups.a: Then dot product equals cosine, which is right for cosine trained models and wrong for dot product trained ones.

q: What is capped Recall@100, and why did your recall differ from the paper on NFCorpus?
plain: Plain Recall@100 is the share of all relevant documents that appear in the top 100. Capped recall divides by the smaller of 100 and the number of relevant documents, so a query with 150 relevant documents can still score a perfect 1. The two agree whenever a query has fewer than 100 relevant documents, which is every SciFact query but not every NFCorpus query. The BEIR paper's appendix reports capped recall, and the replication reports plain recall from pytrec_eval. So small NFCorpus recall differences can come from the metric definition, not the model.
deep: $\text{R@k} = |\text{Rel} \cap \text{Top}_k| / |\text{Rel}|$; $\text{R}_{\text{cap}}@k = |\text{Rel} \cap \text{Top}_k| / \min(k, |\text{Rel}|)$. NFCorpus averages 38.2 judged documents per query, and some queries exceed 100, so plain recall can be lower than capped. README values: BM25 NFCorpus R@100 published 0.25, reproduced 0.246; TAS-B 0.28 and 0.280; DPR 0.208 and 0.208. Fix listed as next step: report capped recall to match Table 12.
say: Plain recall at 100 is the fraction of all relevant documents that show up in the top hundred. Capped recall divides by the smaller of a hundred and the number of relevant documents, so a query with 150 relevant documents can still reach one. The two are identical when a query has fewer than a hundred relevant documents, which is true for every SciFact query but not for every NFCorpus query. The paper's appendix reports capped recall, and I report plain recall from pytrec_eval, so any small NFCorpus recall gap could be the definition rather than the model. Reporting capped recall is on my list of changes.
must_mention: plain recall divides by all relevant
capped divides by min of k and relevant

followups.q: Why would anyone cap recall?
followups.a: So queries with very many relevant documents are not impossible to score well on at k.

q: Why did NFCorpus hide the DPR bug that SciFact exposed?
plain: NFCorpus has about 38 relevant documents per query, so even a damaged ranking still puts several in the top 10. SciFact has about one per query, so losing that one document wipes out the query's score. Think of a quiz with one right answer per question against one with thirty right answers per question. Miss one item and the first quiz scores zero while the second barely notices.
deep: nDCG@10 $= \text{DCG@10}/\text{IDCG@10}$ with $\text{DCG} = \sum_{i} g(\text{rel}_i)/\log_2(i+1)$ over the top 10, where trec_eval uses the judged relevance as the gain. With 38.2 judged documents per query, many relevant documents compete for the top 10, so truncation that degrades the embedding still lands some of them there: DPR reproduced at 0.191 against 0.189 regardless. With 1.1 judged documents per query, the score depends on one document's rank; if truncation drops it below 10, the query scores 0. Sparse judgement datasets are the sensitive instrument; a single dense judgement dataset would have hidden the bug.
say: It's about how many relevant documents each query has. NFCorpus has 38.2 judged documents per query, so even if truncation damages the embeddings, a few relevant ones still land in the top ten and nDCG at 10 barely moves. DPR reproduced there at 0.191 against 0.189 with the bug in place. SciFact has 1.1 judged documents per query, so each query's score hangs on one document: push it out of the top ten and that query scores zero. That makes SciFact the sensitive instrument. The general lesson is that you want at least one evaluation set with sparse judgements, because a dense one can absorb a real bug.
must_mention: one relevant document per query is sensitive

followups.q: How would you formalise the sensitivity?
followups.a: Simulate random demotions of relevant documents and compare the variance of nDCG@10 across the two datasets.

traps: Blaming dataset size alone.

q: What would you change about the BEIR replication?
plain: Run the official Lucene based BM25 so the baseline is identical, report recall the way the paper does, add more datasets, and add an automatic check for embedders truncating documents. The guiding idea is to make the baseline identical to the paper's, so any remaining gap is about the models. The truncation check turns one bug into a guard for every future retrieval project.
deep: Changes in order of value: Anserini BM25 (needs Java) to remove the plus 0.012 and minus 0.005 BM25 gaps that likely come from one concatenated field and exact document lengths; capped Recall@100 as in Table 12; more BEIR datasets with sparse judgements, since those expose ranking damage; a cross encoder rerank row; a guard comparing each model's max_seq_length with the corpus token length distribution.
say: First, I'd run the real Anserini BM25. Mine is a Python reimplementation with the same parameters, but it concatenates title and body into one field and uses exact document lengths where Lucene quantises them, which is the likely source of my plus 0.012 and minus 0.005. Second, I'd report capped recall the way the paper's appendix does, since plain recall differs on some NFCorpus queries. Third, more datasets with few judged documents per query, because those are the ones sensitive enough to expose bugs. And I'd add an automatic check that compares every embedder's token limit against the actual document lengths, since the DPR failure exists in any RAG system with long chunks.

followups.q: Why does the truncation check generalise?
followups.a: Any RAG pipeline whose chunks exceed the embedder's configured limit silently embeds only a prefix.

traps: Proposing to tune until the numbers match.

q: What are the weak spots of your BEIR replication?

The BM25 is a Python reimplementation, which likely explains the plus 0.012 and minus 0.005 differences. And two results, bge-small and hybrid RRF, are extensions that the paper never tested, so they must never be called reproductions. Owning them looks like stating each with its cause and its fix.

Fix one README sentence: it says BM25 beats every dense model evaluated on these datasets, but its own table lists ColBERT at 0.671 on SciFact against 0.665. Also be ready for the two 100 token numbers: 0.260 (first run) and 0.276 (sweep with title [SEP] text encoding).

q: Give me the Dr. GRPO replication in one sentence.

q: Walk me through the Dr. GRPO replication.

q: Take me through the Dr. GRPO replication in depth.

I used the paper's own model, template, grader and data, and paired the arms: same 16 questions every step, same 500 eval problems. To fit free GPUs I used LoRA rank 64, a 1024 token budget and 100 steps. On seed 0, Dr. GRPO ran 99 tokens longer per step, wrong answers 680 against 545, while accuracy held at 51.6 against 51.2 percent. GRPO's correct answers were shorter, so half the mechanism showed. q: Explain why GRPO's length normalisation could make wrong answers longer.
plain: GRPO divides each response's loss by its own length, so every response gets the same total push regardless of length. For a wrong answer, a longer one spreads the same penalty over more tokens, so each token is penalised less, which can let wrong answers drift longer. Imagine a fine split evenly across every word of an answer: a longer wrong answer pays less per word.
deep: Per token gradient weight: GRPO $-A/|o|$, Dr. GRPO $-A/B$ with $B$ the budget. Summed over the response, GRPO gives total $A$ for any length; Dr. GRPO gives $A|o|/B$. Example with $A=-1$, $B=1024$: GRPO gives $-0.01$ per token at 100 tokens and $-0.0025$ at 400; Dr. GRPO gives about $-0.00098$ per token at both, so the 400 token wrong answer carries four times the total penalty. Symmetrically, for correct answers ($A>0$) GRPO rewards each token of a short answer more, pushing correct answers shorter. The std term divides advantages by the group's reward std, upweighting near solved or near hopeless questions (rewards 1,1,1,0 give advantages about 0.58 and minus 1.73). In the replication's seed 0, the correct answer side appeared (262 against 399 tokens) and the wrong answer side did not.
say: GRPO averages each response's token losses over that response's own length. So the total push on a response is the same whatever its length, and per token it's the advantage divided by the length. For a wrong answer with advantage minus one, a 100 token response gets minus 0.01 per token, but a 400 token one only minus 0.0025, so the long wrong answer is penalised less per token and there's less pressure to stop rambling. Dr. GRPO divides by a fixed budget instead, so the longer wrong answer carries four times the total penalty. The same logic predicts GRPO makes correct answers shorter, and in my seed that half did show up.

per token penalty smaller for long wrong answers
Dr. GRPO divides by a fixed budget
correct answer side appeared, wrong answer side did not

followups.q: What does the std normalisation do?
followups.a: Divides advantages by the group's reward std, so questions with nearly all right or all wrong responses get larger advantages.

followups.q: How did you verify the gradient?
followups.a: Unit tests that the per token gradient is exactly minus A over length under GRPO and minus A over budget under Dr. GRPO.

traps: Claiming the replication confirmed the wrong answer mechanism.

q: How did you make sure your RL trainer was correct before trusting the result?
plain: By testing each piece against something independent before running the experiment. The loss was checked against its closed form gradient, two implementations of it were checked against each other, and the batched log probabilities were checked against a slow high precision version. During training, the sampler's and learner's probabilities for the same tokens were compared every step to confirm the policy being sampled was the policy being trained. Done well, a replication can say which checks would have caught which bugs. Done badly, it trusts a loss curve that goes down.
deep: Checks from the README: per token gradient exactly $-A/|o|$ under GRPO and $-A/B$ under Dr. GRPO (tests/test_objective.py, tests/test_objective_torch.py); PyTorch and MLX losses agree to 1e-6 on identical inputs; batched, padded log probabilities match an fp64 per sequence forward to 1e-5, which also caught that PyTorch's CPU log_softmax is off by 1.7e-4 over a 151,936 token vocabulary; merged LoRA weights reproduce the adapter model's outputs; sampler and learner log probabilities differed by only 0.002 to 0.004 nats per step.

Batched, padded log probabilities match a slow fp64 forward to 1e-5, which incidentally caught PyTorch's CPU log softmax being slightly off over a 151,936 token vocabulary. Merged LoRA weights reproduce the adapter's outputs. And during training, the sampler and learner disagreed by only 0.002 to 0.004 nats, so I was training the policy I was sampling.

The smaller 0.5B model scored 0 of 128 under the strict answer format, which gives GRPO no reward signal at all, so 1.5B was used, which is also the paper's figure model. q: What engineering problems did you hit in the Dr. GRPO replication?

q: Give me handoff in one sentence.
plain: The 15 second version is: handoff is a supervisor agent system for incident response in which every escalation has an owner, a deadline and a declared behaviour for silence, so an unanswered page runs a safer substitute instead of hanging. The memorable image is the 3am page nobody answers. Done well, it names the problem (confirm dialogs that block forever) and the fix in one breath. Done badly, it starts with the five worker types.
deep: Core claim from the README: escalation is a routing problem with deadlines, ownership and a declared behaviour for silence. The demo case: failover_database (high risk, irreversible) pages the primary with 180 seconds; on expiry the declared substitute enable_read_only runs. The domain (incident response on a simulated cluster) is not the point; the escalation layer is.
say: handoff is an agent system for incident response where every request for human approval has an owner, a deadline and a written down behaviour for when nobody answers. Most human in the loop is a confirm dialog that blocks forever, and at three in the morning the realistic case is silence. So if a risky failover isn't approved in time, the system runs the tool's declared safer substitute, putting the database into read only mode, instead of either waiting forever or going ahead unreviewed. The incident domain is just the setting; the escalation layer is the project.

q: Walk me through handoff.
plain: An incident response agent system where every escalation to a human has a deadline and a declared behaviour if nobody answers, so an unanswered request runs a safer action instead of hanging. Think of an on call page that, if nobody answers, automatically takes the safe option. Failing a database over is risky and irreversible, while switching it to read only loses nothing and can be undone.
deep: Supervisor plus five workers (four report, one proposes); only the supervisor can call mutating tools. Tools declare risk, reversibility, blast radius and a strictly safer substitute, validated at import. Policy as YAML: medium 300 s then escalate; high 180 s then safe fallback; critical 600 s, hold, quorum 2. Contested hypotheses raise action risk one level. Caller driven tick, no background threads. 200 tests and 11 scenarios passing, 0.08 to 0.10 s, 3,666 source lines in 35 modules, 15 tools, no dependencies; simulated cluster, rule based workers.
say: handoff is a supervisor agent system for incident response where escalations have deadlines. Most human in the loop is a confirm dialog that blocks forever, and what actually happens at 3am is that nobody answers. Here each tool declares its risk, whether it's reversible, its blast radius and a strictly safer substitute, and policy is a YAML table: a high risk action pages the primary with 180 seconds to answer, and on expiry runs the safer fallback. So an unanswered database failover becomes read only mode, which loses no in flight transactions and a human can undo. No expiry rule can approve an action nobody looked at. The cluster is simulated and the workers are rule based; it has 200 tests and no dependencies.

q: Why can't your escalation policy approve an action when the deadline expires?
plain: Because a timeout is not a decision. Letting silence approve an irreversible action means nobody looked at it. The allowed expiry behaviours are escalate, run a safer substitute, drop, or hold. A timeout means nobody looked, so treating it as a yes would run the riskiest actions exactly when nobody is watching.
deep: ADR 0004: OnExpiry has four members (escalate up the ladder, safe fallback, deny, hold) and none approves. Load time validation refuses a rule requiring approval without on_expiry, a quorum larger than its ladder, a ladder tier nobody stands on, and a safe fallback that does not check out. The journal records that a fallback ran because nobody answered, distinct from a human approving. Trade off: when the original action was right, the system is slower to take it.
say: Because silence isn't consent. If a timeout could approve a database failover, the most dangerous actions would run exactly when nobody is watching. So the policy has four expiry behaviours: escalate to the next tier, run the tool's declared safer substitute, drop the action, or freeze the incident, and none of them approves. The journal records that the fallback ran because nobody answered, which is a different fact from a person deciding it. The trade off is real: when the original action was the right one, we're slower to take it. I accept that, because a reversible degraded state is recoverable and an unreviewed irreversible action may not be.
must_mention: slower when the action was right

followups.q: What stops a misconfigured policy?
followups.a: Four checks at load time, including a fallback that is not actually lower risk.

traps: Saying a long enough timeout makes approval safe.

q: Why does handoff raise risk when its workers disagree?
plain: Because uncertainty about the diagnosis and danger in the fix have the same remedy: ask a person. The aggregator tracks which workers support and which contradict each hypothesis, and one with confident voices on both sides is marked contested. Any action addressing a contested hypothesis has its effective risk raised by one level, so a low risk restart that would normally run unattended stops and asks. Averaging the votes would hide exactly the disagreement a human should see. Done well, you give the restart example.
deep: Mechanism: hypotheses carry supporting and contradicting worker sets with confidence; contested equals confident support and confident contradiction. Effective risk equals declared risk plus one for actions on contested hypotheses, then the policy rule for the effective risk applies. One of the three kept bugs was here: the planner was fed only confirmed hypotheses, so contested ones produced no proposal and the risk raising branch was unreachable; another was looking up the rule by declared rather than effective risk.
say: Because a confident disagreement between workers is information a human should see, not something to average away. If the log analyst sees a high error rate and the metrics analyst sees healthy latency, both confidently, the hypothesis is contested. Any action addressing it gets its effective risk raised one level, so a low risk restart that would normally just run now stops and asks. Uncertainty about what's wrong and danger in the fix are different problems with the same remedy. Two of the bugs I kept in the history were exactly here, which is a good sign the mechanism is worth testing.
must_mention: contested equals confident support and contradiction

followups.q: What was the bug?
followups.a: Contested hypotheses never reached the planner, so the risk raising code was unreachable: a guarantee that was decoration.

traps: Describing it as majority voting.

q: How do you test a 180 second deadline without waiting 180 seconds?
plain: Make time an input. In handoff nothing sleeps and nothing runs on a background thread; the caller drives a tick function with the current time, so a test can jump the clock to exactly the deadline and check which side of it the decision falls on. That is why every deadline is tested at its exact boundary and the whole suite runs in about a tenth of a second. The cost is that a real deployment needs a scheduler to call tick, which is deliberately missing. Done well, you name both the benefit and the missing piece.
deep: Design (ADR 0003, escalation is a policy, not a callback): deadlines are data on pending escalations; tick(now) evaluates expiries and applies on_expiry deterministically. Tests set now to deadline minus epsilon and deadline exactly. Suite: 200 tests, wall time 0.08 to 0.10 s over three runs. Limitation stated in the README: there is no scheduler, and Journal.subscribe is where a pager would attach but nothing does.
say: I make time an input instead of something the code waits for. Nothing in handoff sleeps or runs on a background thread; the caller drives a tick function with the current time. So a test can set the clock to one moment before the deadline, check the request is still pending, then set it to exactly the deadline and check the fallback ran. Every deadline gets tested at its exact boundary, and the whole suite of 200 tests runs in about a tenth of a second. The trade off is that in a deployment something has to call tick on a timer, and that scheduler is deliberately not built yet.
must_mention: suite in about a tenth of a second

followups.q: Where would the pager attach?
followups.a: Journal.subscribe, which nothing attaches to yet.

traps: Using real sleeps in tests.

q: Tell me about a bug in handoff that taught you something.
plain: handoff keeps three bugs in its history because each is a category of mistake this kind of system invites. The best one is safety code that could not run: the risk raising branch for contested diagnoses was unreachable because the planner only received confirmed hypotheses. It read like a guarantee and was decoration. The second looked up the policy rule by the tool's declared low risk after deciding to escalate, so an empty ladder dropped the action, which reads in the journal like a deliberate decision. The third was a config parser that flattened nested maps, caught only because a modify decision rejects missing arguments.
deep: Lessons per bug: (1) unreachable safety code needs an end to end scenario, not a unit test of the branch; (2) a dropped action must be distinguishable from a policy decision in the audit trail; (3) strict validation at consumption points surfaces silent config corruption. All three were found by scenarios and validation, and are kept rather than squashed in the commit history.
say: My favourite is safety code that couldn't run. handoff raises the risk of an action when workers disagree about the diagnosis, and that branch had unit tests. But the planner was only ever given confirmed hypotheses, so a contested diagnosis never produced a proposal, and the risk raising code was unreachable through the normal flow. It read like a guarantee and was decoration. The lesson was that a safety mechanism needs an end to end scenario that drives it, not just a test of the function. I kept it in the commit history, along with two related bugs, because each is a mistake this kind of system invites.

followups.q: What were the other two?
followups.a: A rule looked up by declared rather than effective risk, which silently dropped actions; and a parser that flattened nested config.

traps: Choosing a trivial typo as the bug story.

q: Take me through the distributed ViT project in depth.
plain: The six beats: most distributed speedups cannot be checked; the project makes them checkable; a hand written ViT with DDP, FSDP, mixed precision and accumulation; the decision to isolate the regression with synthetic inputs rather than tune workers; the results across three hardware groups; and better input pipelines next. Speedup is only ever computed against a baseline on the same hardware that differs only in rank count. Done well, the surprise and its isolation take most of the time. Done badly, it lists the hyperparameters.
deep: Model: ViT, 1,806,538 parameters, patch 4 on 32 by 32, about 7 MB of gradients per all reduce. Hardware groups: M5 MPS single device, gloo over 10 CPU cores, Kaggle 2 T4 nccl (the only real speedup measurement). T4 results, 30 epochs: 1,853 and 3,637 img/s fp32 (98 percent); 3,810 and 4,376 fp16 (57 percent); synthetic input 1.92 times at 96 percent; FSDP 0.66 times DDP. MPS: fp16 eager 726 against fp32 1,061; compiled fp16 2,361 (2.23 times). gloo 1 to 4 ranks: 552 to 879 img/s, which contradicted the predicted slowdown, so the prediction was deleted. make verify traces every unit bearing number in README, RESULTS and CLAUDE.md to artifacts; it found five unsupported claims on first run.

The model is a hand written ViT, about 1.8 million parameters, which means each all reduce moves only about 7 megabytes. I tested gradient equivalence between one and two ranks in a real process group. On two T4s, fp32 scaled at 98 percent, but fp16 fell to 57. Rather than fiddle with dataloader workers, I added a synthetic input mode that removes decoding entirely, and it restored 96 percent, so the CPUs, not the all reduce, were the bottleneck. Every number traces to a run artifact through a verify script that caught five unsupported claims the first time it ran. Next is a faster input pipeline.

verify script found five unsupported claims

q: How do you know the two GPU run trains the same model as the one GPU run?
plain: DDP averages gradients across GPUs, so two GPUs each with half the batch should give exactly the gradient of one GPU with the full batch. A test checks that identity in a real process group, and a second test computes it wrongly to prove the check can fail. It is like averaging two class averages to get the school average: it works only when the classes are the same size.
deep: With mean reduced loss and equal per rank batch $B$, $\frac{1}{R}\sum_r \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in r}\nabla\ell_i = \frac{1}{RB}\sum_i \nabla\ell_i$. It fails with unequal per rank batches (a quick numeric check with 100 and 156 examples does not match the global mean), sum reduced losses without rescaling, or rank dependent augmentation without matched seeds. tests/test_ddp_equivalence.py spawns a real gloo group and compares to rtol 1e-4; an inverse test computes the wrong reduction and must fail. Baseline discipline: a rank scaling baseline differs in exactly one property, the rank count.
say: Because DDP averages gradients. If each of two ranks holds a batch of B and the loss is a mean, the average of their two mean gradients equals the mean gradient over all 2B examples, which is what one process with the doubled batch computes. I test exactly that: the suite spawns a real gloo process group and compares the gradients to a relative tolerance of 1e-4. And it ships with a twin test that deliberately computes the wrong reduction, because a correctness test that can't fail is decoration. The identity breaks with unequal batches per rank or a summed loss, so I also make sure the scaling baseline differs only in the number of ranks.
must_mention: mean of rank means equals global mean with equal batches
baseline differs only in rank count

followups.q: When does the identity fail?
followups.a: Unequal per rank batch sizes, sum reduction without rescaling, or rank dependent randomness.

followups.q: Why gloo for the test?
followups.a: It runs on CPU, so correctness is testable on a laptop with no GPUs.

traps: Assuming equivalence because the loss curves look similar.

q: Why does gradient accumulation under DDP need no_sync()?
plain: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several small batches before one optimiser step, to get a large effective batch without the memory. Under DDP, every backward pass normally triggers an all reduce across GPUs. Without no_sync(), you pay a full all reduce for every microbatch, so accumulation makes training slower instead of cheaper. Wrapping all but the last microbatch in no_sync() skips the communication until the final one. Done well, you also say the gradients must be scaled so the accumulated sum equals the mean over the effective batch.
deep: With $m$ microbatches, communication drops from $m$ all reduces per step to 1. Loss scaling: divide each microbatch loss by $m$ (for equal microbatch sizes) so the accumulated gradient equals the mean over the effective batch. The README's engine.py implements accumulation inside no_sync() for non final microbatches. A related distinction: DDP overlaps the all reduce with the backward pass in buckets, which is why a small model's 7 MB gradient payload was not the bottleneck.
say: Because DDP all reduces gradients after every backward pass by default. If I accumulate over four microbatches without no_sync, I pay four full all reduces for one optimiser step, so accumulation, which was supposed to buy a big effective batch cheaply, makes the job slower. Wrapping the first three microbatches in no_sync skips their communication, and only the last backward triggers the all reduce of the summed gradients. I also divide each microbatch loss by the number of microbatches, so the accumulated gradient is the mean over the effective batch, and the update matches a true large batch.
must_mention: scale loss by number of microbatches

followups.q: Does accumulation change the result versus a real big batch?
followups.a: Not for plain SGD with mean losses; batch norm statistics are the usual exception.

traps: Forgetting to scale the loss.

q: Why did fp16 reduce scaling efficiency if the communication volume did not change?
plain: Scaling efficiency is speedup divided by ideal speedup, so it depends on everything in the step, not only communication. fp16 roughly halved the GPU compute time per batch, which left the fixed host side work, decoding and augmenting images on four CPU cores, as a much larger share of each step. With two GPUs, the CPUs could not prepare data fast enough, so the second GPU waited. Removing the dataloader with synthetic inputs restored 96 percent, which rules out the all reduce. Done well, you say efficiency is a property of the whole pipeline, not of the interconnect.
deep: Efficiency $E = S/R$ with $S = T_1/T_R$. Measured: fp32 $3637/1853 \approx 1.963$, $E \approx 98.1$ percent; fp16 $4376/3810 \approx 1.149$, $E \approx 57.4$ percent (both checked). Model: per step time $t = \max(t_{gpu}, t_{host}) + t_{comm,exposed}$; halving $t_{gpu}$ makes $t_{host}$ binding when two ranks share four vCPUs. Isolation: synthetic in memory tensors (no decode, augmentation or workers) gave 1.92 times at 96 percent. The prediction written beforehand (DDP near 1.8 times because the all reduce would dominate a small model) was backwards: small gradients overlap with backward almost entirely.
say: Because efficiency is a property of the whole step, not of the network between GPUs. Efficiency is the speedup divided by the number of GPUs. In fp32, two GPUs gave 1.96 times, 98 percent. Mixed precision roughly halved the compute per batch, so the fixed host work, decoding and augmenting images on Kaggle's four CPU cores, became the bottleneck, and with two GPUs to feed the second one waited for data. The communication volume was identical and, at 7 megabytes, overlaps with the backward pass. The proof was the synthetic input run, which removes decoding entirely and restored 96 percent. Optimising one layer just moved the bottleneck.

host decode on four vCPUs became binding

followups.a: That DDP would land near 1.8 times because the all reduce would dominate; it was backwards, and the prediction is recorded as wrong.

followups.q: How would you fix it?
followups.a: Pre decoded tensors or GPU side augmentation, or a host with more cores.

traps: Blaming nccl without isolating it.

q: How did you stop yourself from quoting wrong numbers or faking a topology?

q: Walk me through the tool dependency graph.
plain: A graph built from 1,391 tool descriptions that tells an AI agent which tools must run before which, and which inputs must be asked of the user, because agents fail when they need an ID only another tool can provide. For example, replying to an email thread needs a thread id that only a 'list threads' tool can produce, so the graph records that list threads must run first. A subject line, by contrast, is something the user writes, so the agent should ask for it.
deep: Bipartite graph of tools and namespaced entities (gmail.thread_id); three tier path resolution (leaf, nearest meaningful ancestor, producing tool's object); primary versus incidental producers by head noun and depth; slot buckets (tool derived, user supplied, control, enum, unresolved). Results on a production catalog: 1,391 tools, 46 entities, 3,278 edges, 7,101 slots with 2,728 required, 1,770 of 2,728 (65 percent) resolved, 1,768 of 1,770 (99.9 percent) with a producer, slug fallback fired 0 times, 568 unresolved. Eight assertions in check.py.
say: Agents fail tool calls for a boring reason: they need an argument they can't produce, like a thread id that only a listing call returns. I built a dependency graph from 1,391 tool schemas across two large toolkits that says which tools must run first and which inputs must come from the user. Matching names fails three ways: generic names like id collide across services, a bare id's meaning lives in its parent path, and responses embed almost every object. So handles resolve to namespaced entities, paths resolve in three tiers, and producers are ranked by the head noun of the tool's name. Of 2,728 required inputs, 65 percent resolve to an entity, and 99.9 percent of those have a producer.

q: Why is the tool dependency graph bipartite?

q: How does the ZTF pipeline monitor drift, and why monitor predictions rather than accuracy?
plain: It computes the population stability index of the model's prediction distribution over time. PSI compares how predictions are spread across bins today against a reference period, and a large value means the model is seeing something different. Monitoring predictions matters because true labels for astronomical alerts arrive late or never, so accuracy cannot be measured in time to act. Done well, you say drift in predictions is a warning, not proof that the model got worse. Done badly, you call it accuracy monitoring.
deep: $\text{PSI} = \sum_b (p_b - q_b)\ln(p_b/q_b)$ over bins $b$, with $q$ the reference distribution and $p$ the current one. A common rule of thumb treats values above about 0.25 as a large shift, but thresholds are conventions to tune per system. Prediction drift can come from input shift (new survey conditions), upstream bugs (a broken feature) or real astrophysical changes; it says to look, not what is wrong. The monitoring mart (mart_model_monitoring) holds the rollup.
say: It tracks the population stability index of the prediction distribution: how the share of predictions in each score bin today compares with a reference period. A big shift means the model is seeing something different. I monitor predictions rather than accuracy because labels for astronomical alerts arrive late or never, so by the time you could measure accuracy the problem is old news. The caveat is that prediction drift is a warning, not a diagnosis; it could be new observing conditions, a broken upstream feature or something real in the sky, and you still have to look.

q: Why does logistic regression get 0.95 AUC but only 0.31 F1 in ShopFloor AI?
plain: AUC and F1 measure different things. AUC asks how well the model ranks failing machines above healthy ones across every possible threshold, while F1 is measured at one threshold and balances precision and recall there. With only 3.39 percent failures, a model can rank well overall yet, at the default threshold, flag too few real failures or too many false alarms. So logistic regression at 0.9455 AUC and 0.3054 F1 is not a contradiction. Tuning its threshold or reweighting classes would raise its F1, and a precision recall curve would show the trade off directly.
deep: ROC AUC equals the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative; it is insensitive to class imbalance in a way that can flatter models when positives are rare. F1 $= 2PR/(P+R)$ at a chosen threshold. Under heavy imbalance, PR AUC (average precision) is more informative because its baseline is the positive rate (here 0.0339) rather than 0.5. The same logic explains why random forest can have the higher ROC AUC (0.9823) and lower F1 (0.8387) than gradient boosting (0.9591, 0.8548).

q: Walk me through media-pulse and comms-agent.

Both run on synthetic data. The idea is that the model handles the confident cases and people check the uncertain tail, like a spell checker that only asks about words it is unsure of.
deep: media-pulse: pluggable ingestion, VADER and TF-IDF with logistic regression (numpy fallbacks), confidence per prediction, review queue with immutable audit log, comms metrics (share of voice weighted by reach, message pull through, sentiment over time), model QA (held out accuracy, ECE, accuracy by outlet type). Synthetic 120 mention corpus, about 30 percent spanning two topics: topic 0.88 to 0.96 and sentiment 0.50 to 0.85 after review. comms-agent: state graph with retries, max step guard, trace; 9 of 24 flagged, 7 corrected; MockLLM and oracle reviewer.
say: media-pulse is a communications measurement system. It ingests brand mentions, classifies each for sentiment and topic with a confidence attached, sends anything below a threshold to a human review queue with an immutable audit log, and reports share of voice, message pull through and sentiment, plus a review of the classifier's own calibration and accuracy by outlet type. On a synthetic corpus of 120 mentions, review lifted held out topic accuracy from about 0.88 to 0.96. comms-agent runs that loop as an explicit state graph with a conditional review gate; on 24 sample mentions it flagged 9 and the reviewer corrected 7. The data is synthetic and the reviewer is simulated, so it demonstrates the loop, not real world accuracy.

followups.q: Why a state graph?
followups.a: Explicit, testable control flow with zero dependencies; it maps onto LangGraph.

followups.q: What would you measure with real reviewers?
followups.a: Inter reviewer agreement and time per item.

traps: Presenting the uplift as a real world result.

q: Take me through media-pulse and comms-agent in depth.
plain: The six beats: comms teams act on classifier output that is wrong on the hard tail; they need to know which numbers a person checked; pluggable ingestion, classification with confidences, a review queue, metrics and a model QA review, plus an agent graph; the decision of where to set the confidence threshold; results on synthetic data with the oracle caveat; and real data, a real review UI and an LLM classifier next. The threshold decision trades reviewer time against errors left in the report. Done well, you explain why calibration error is reported alongside accuracy.
deep: media-pulse: SampleSource (120 labelled synthetic mentions; about 30 percent span two topics) and an RSSAdapter on one Article schema; VADER sentiment and TF-IDF with logistic regression topic when installed, numpy fallbacks otherwise; message pull through and relevance; review.py queue with immutable audit log; metrics.py comms metrics plus accuracy, ECE and subgroup accuracy by outlet type; Streamlit four tab dashboard. Reported on held out synthetic data: topic about 0.88 to 0.96, sentiment about 0.50 to 0.85 after review. comms-agent: orchestrator.py with named nodes, fixed and conditional edges, per node retries, max step guard, trace; 9 of 24 flagged, 7 corrected by an oracle backed reviewer.
say: Comms teams act on classifier numbers that are wrong exactly on the hard cases, and they need to know which numbers a person checked. media-pulse attaches a confidence to every sentiment and topic prediction, routes anything below a threshold to a review queue, overwrites the label with the correction and logs it immutably. It also reviews the model: held out accuracy, calibration error and accuracy by outlet type. The key choice is the threshold, which trades reviewer time against errors left in the report, and calibration is what makes that threshold meaningful. comms-agent runs the loop as a state graph with retries and a trace. It's synthetic data with a simulated reviewer, so real reviewers are next.

followups.q: What does accuracy by outlet type show?
followups.a: Where the model is weakest, which may justify a lower threshold for that subgroup.

traps: Ignoring the oracle caveat.

q: How much of media-pulse's accuracy uplift from human review is real?
plain: Less than the headline suggests. With synthetic data and a simulated reviewer, corrections are always right, so the uplift mostly measures how many wrong predictions the confidence threshold managed to catch. If the reviewer is always right, accuracy after review is just accuracy before review plus the mistakes the threshold happened to route to the reviewer.
deep: Decompose: final accuracy equals base accuracy plus the share of errors that fall below the confidence threshold (if corrections are perfect). So the uplift measures confidence separation (a calibration and ranking property), not human performance. Real reviewers disagree and tire; measure inter reviewer agreement, review time, and accuracy of corrected labels. The 0.50 sentiment baseline also indicates a weak default model on this corpus. The calibration review (ECE) matters because routing depends on confidence.
say: Honestly, part of it is built in. The corpus is synthetic and in the demo the reviewer is effectively an oracle, so every correction is right. That means the uplift, topic accuracy from about 0.88 to 0.96, mostly measures how many of the model's mistakes fell below the confidence threshold, which is really a property of how well the confidence scores separate right from wrong. That's still useful, and it's why the project reports calibration error. But real reviewers disagree and get tired, so with real data I'd measure agreement between reviewers and time per item before claiming any uplift. The 0.50 sentiment baseline also tells me the default sentiment model is weak here.

followups.q: What threshold would you pick?
followups.a: The one that meets an accuracy target for the report at an acceptable review load, read off a calibration curve.

traps: Claiming humans improved accuracy by 35 points.

q: Why does media-pulse report expected calibration error, and how is it computed?
plain: Because the review gate routes items by confidence, the confidences have to mean what they say. Expected calibration error measures the gap between how confident the model claims to be and how often it is actually right. You sort predictions into confidence bins, compare each bin's average confidence with its accuracy, and take the weighted average of the gaps. If predictions labelled 90 percent confident are right only 70 percent of the time, the gate will trust items it should route to a person. Done well, you connect calibration directly to the routing rule.
deep: $\text{ECE} = \sum_{b} \frac{n_b}{N} \lvert \text{acc}(b) - \text{conf}(b) \rvert$ over $B$ equal width bins. Caveats: depends on the number of bins and is noisy on small held out sets; report a reliability diagram alongside. Fixes for miscalibration: temperature scaling or isotonic regression on a validation split. Routing: with calibrated scores, the expected number of errors left after review at threshold $t$ is the sum of $(1 - c_i)$ over items with confidence above $t$, which lets you choose $t$ for a target report accuracy.
say: Because the review gate routes on confidence, so the confidence has to be honest. Expected calibration error compares what the model claims with how often it's right: group predictions into confidence bins, compare each bin's average confidence with its accuracy, and average the gaps weighted by bin size. If items scored 90 percent confident are right only 70 percent of the time, the gate waves through mistakes it should send to a person. With calibrated scores, I can even estimate how many errors stay in the report at a given threshold, and pick the threshold for a target accuracy. On small test sets ECE is noisy, so I'd show a reliability diagram too.
must_mention: estimate errors left at a threshold

followups.q: How would you fix miscalibration?
followups.a: Temperature scaling or isotonic regression on a validation split.

traps: Treating accuracy as enough for a confidence gate.

q: Tell me about your Wikipedia edit stream dashboard.
plain: A live page that counts every Wikipedia edit two ways, exactly and with compact streaming sketches, and plots how far each sketch drifts from the truth. A sketch is a small data structure that estimates a count without storing every item, trading a little accuracy for a lot of memory. Running an exact counter beside each sketch shows the error as it happens.
deep: HyperLogLog p = 12 (4,096 one byte registers, MurmurHash3) for distinct editors, standard error about $1.04/\sqrt{4096} \approx 1.6$ percent; Count-Min 4 by 1,024 with $\varepsilon = e/1024 \approx 0.27$ percent of N and $\delta = e^{-4} \approx 1.8$ percent; Space-Saving with 200 counters, every item above N/k tracked, count minus error at most true at most count. Runs on October 8, 2026: 297 s, 9,909 events, HLL 986.9 against 983 (plus 0.4 percent), 0 Space-Saving violations, Count-Min top 12 within eps N. Burst detection moved to event time bins after arrival time binning flagged delivery clumps.
say: It counts every Wikipedia edit twice: exactly, and with streaming sketches that fit in a few kilobytes, so you can watch the error live. HyperLogLog with 4,096 registers estimates distinct editors, Count-Min counts edits per wiki, and Space-Saving with 200 counters tracks the busiest pages with an error bound on each. In a logged 297 second run with 9,909 events, HyperLogLog said 986.9 distinct editors against an exact 983, plus 0.4 percent, inside its roughly 1.6 percent standard error, and Space-Saving had zero bound violations. One real lesson: binning by arrival time flagged delivery clumps as bursts, so the chart now bins by each edit's own timestamp.

followups.q: Is Count-Min stressed here?
followups.a: Barely: about 100 wikis in 1,024 columns rarely collide, and the README says so.

traps: Claiming the sketches were needed at 30 events a second.

q: What error bounds do HyperLogLog, Count-Min and Space-Saving promise?
plain: Each sketch trades exactness for tiny memory, with a known error. HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts with a relative standard error of about 1.04 over the square root of its register count, about 1.6 percent with 4,096 registers. Count-Min never undercounts, and with high probability overcounts by at most a small share of all events, set by its width and depth. Space-Saving with k counters keeps every item seen more than N over k times and gives each count a known error. In the Wikipedia run, HyperLogLog was off by 0.4 percent, well inside one standard error.
deep: HyperLogLog: $\sigma \approx 1.04/\sqrt{m}$; $m = 4096$ gives $\approx 1.625$ percent; linear counting below about $2.5m$ (README: switch near 10,240 distinct editors). Count-Min with width $w$ and depth $d$: $\hat f \ge f$ and $\hat f \le f + \varepsilon N$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, $\varepsilon = e/w$, $\delta = e^{-d}$; for $w = 1024$, $d = 4$: $\varepsilon \approx 0.27$ percent, $\delta \approx 1.8$ percent. Space-Saving with $k$ counters: count minus error at most true at most count; items above $N/k$ guaranteed present (for the 297 s run, $9909/200 \approx 49.5$ edits). Measured: 986.9 against 983, 0 violations, 12 of 12 within $\varepsilon N$.
say: HyperLogLog estimates distinct items with a relative standard error of about 1.04 over the square root of the number of registers, so with 4,096 registers it's about 1.6 percent; my run was off by 0.4 percent. Count-Min never undercounts, and with probability at least one minus e to the minus depth it overcounts by at most e over the width times the total count; with 1,024 columns and four rows that's about 0.27 percent of all events, failing under 2 percent of the time. Space-Saving with k counters guarantees anything seen more than N over k times is tracked, with count minus error at or below the truth. I checked all three live against exact counters.
must_mention: Count-Min never undercounts, e over width
Space-Saving keeps items above N over k

followups.q: Why is Count-Min barely stressed here?
followups.a: About 100 wikis in 1,024 columns rarely collide.

followups.q: When does HyperLogLog switch estimators?
followups.a: From linear counting to the raw estimator at about 10,240 distinct editors in this setup.

traps: Saying Count-Min can undercount.

q: Walk me through the order book dashboard.
plain: A live copy of Kraken's bitcoin order book rebuilt in the browser and verified against the exchange's checksum after every update, with order flow statistics computed only from a book known to be correct. An order book is the list of prices and quantities people are waiting to buy and sell at. A checksum is a fingerprint of the book, so matching it proves your copy is the same as the exchange's.
deep: Snapshot plus deltas at depth 100, sorted arrays with binary search updates, truncation back to subscribed depth (the exchange stops updating levels that fall out of range), CRC32 over the top 10 levels formatted with the instrument's precision, resubscribe on mismatch. Runs: 46,892 of 46,892 checksums in 330 s (about 142 updates a second), 0 resyncs. Order flow imbalance (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov 2014) per second regressed on mid change over 300 s: slope 1.10 USD per BTC (se 0.059), R squared 0.54. Realized vol 27.0 percent at 1 s against 31.9 percent at 10 s, where the 10 s estimate rests on 30 returns. Lag 89 ms median, 143 ms p95, including clock offset.
say: Every trading system starts from a local order book built from a snapshot plus deltas, and the classic failure is silent drift. Kraken publishes a CRC32 of the top ten levels with every update, so the page verifies each message and resubscribes on a mismatch. In a 330 second run it verified 46,892 of 46,892 checksums, about 142 updates a second, with no resyncs. Only then does it compute statistics: order flow imbalance, after Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, regressed on mid price changes gave a slope of 1.10 dollars per bitcoin of net flow and an R squared of 0.54. The honest gap is that a natural mismatch never happened, so resync is tested only by forced corruption.
must_mention: resync tested only by forced corruption

followups.q: Why was 10 second volatility higher than 1 second?
followups.a: The 10 second figure rests on only 30 returns, so the page compares the gap with its sampling error instead of calling it noise.

followups.q: Why does precision formatting matter?
followups.a: The checksum is over formatted strings, so 0.0157 and 0.01570000 differ.

traps: Calling it a trading signal; it is analytics on public data.

q: Walk me through the earthquake statistics dashboard.
plain: A page that computes classic seismology statistics from the past week of USGS earthquakes and logs every revision the catalog makes while you watch. The b-value says how much rarer big earthquakes are: a b of 1 means ten times fewer quakes for each step up in magnitude. The catalog log matters because statistics computed from a live feed inherit every later correction.
deep: Completeness by maximum curvature plus 0.2 (Woessner and Wiemer 2005); b by maximum likelihood $\hat b = \log_{10} e/(\bar M - (M_c - \Delta M/2))$ (Aki 1965 with Utsu's correction); Shi and Bolt (1982) uncertainty; a 200 resample bootstrap re-estimating completeness each time; Gardner-Knopoff windows and an Omori-Utsu MLE fit (Ogata 1983) above 30 aftershocks. October 8, 2026: 1,949 events; California b 0.727 plus or minus 0.033 [0.661, 0.851]; pooled b 0.343 is not physical because magnitude types mix. Coverage check: 93.7 percent over 300 synthetic catalogs; test now requires at least 16 of 20. 45 minutes of polling: 9 new events, 7 revisions, no deletions.
say: Earthquake catalogs change after the fact: magnitudes move, events merge under new ids, and some get deleted, so the page computes classic statistics from the week feed and logs every revision. The b-value, how much rarer bigger quakes are, comes from maximum likelihood with Utsu's binning correction, with the Shi and Bolt uncertainty and a 200 resample bootstrap that re-estimates the completeness magnitude each time. California came out at 0.727, interval 0.661 to 0.851. The pooled 0.343 isn't physical, because the feed mixes magnitude scales, and the page says so. My favourite part: a single seed test failed, and across 300 synthetic catalogs the 95 percent interval covered the truth 93.7 percent of the time.

followups.q: Why did one test fail?
followups.a: A 95 percent interval misses about one time in twenty; the test now requires at least 16 of 20 catalogs to cover.

followups.q: Why no Omori fit?
followups.a: No sequence that week reached 30 aftershocks.

traps: Interpreting the pooled b of 0.343 as geophysics.

q: Walk me through the space weather nowcast.
plain: The live input side of a geomagnetic forecasting model: nine NOAA feeds joined on time, solar wind propagated from the L1 spacecraft to Earth, and the physical quantities that drive geomagnetic activity, with the freshness of every input shown. A spacecraft about 1.5 million km toward the Sun measures the solar wind before it reaches Earth, so the warning time depends on the wind's speed. Dynamic pressure is how hard that wind pushes on Earth's magnetic field.
deep: Ballistic delay from the active spacecraft's ephemeris distance over the sample's speed; dynamic pressure $P = m_p n v^2$; Shue et al. (1998) standoff; Newell et al. (2007) coupling $v^{4/3} B_t^{2/3} \sin^{8/3}(\theta/2)$; Kp with NOAA's G scale. October 8, 2026, 19:38 UTC: SOLAR1 at 1.58 million km, 360 km/s, 5.7 per cubic cm, 1.24 nPa (checked: $1.6726\times10^{-27}\cdot 5.7\times10^{6}\cdot(3.6\times10^{5})^2 \approx 1.24\times10^{-9}$ Pa), 10.9 Earth radii, 73.5 min delay; plasma covered 1,265 of 1,435 minutes. Lessons: NOAA rounds Kp before mapping to G (4.67 is G1, 5.67 is G2); NOAA rewrites recent minutes.
say: My earlier Kp forecasting project trained an LSTM on clean hourly history, but in production a model like that runs on live feeds with gaps, revisions and instrument switches, so this page builds that input side. It joins nine NOAA feeds, propagates each solar wind sample from the L1 spacecraft to Earth using its real distance and the sample's own speed, and computes dynamic pressure, the Shue magnetopause standoff and the Newell coupling function. In one logged pass the wind was 360 kilometres a second, giving 1.24 nanopascals, a standoff of 10.9 Earth radii and arrival 73.5 minutes after measurement. The feeds also corrected my spec: NOAA rounds Kp before mapping it to the G scale.

propagation from L1 by distance and speed

followups.q: How accurate is ballistic propagation?
followups.a: Approximate; tilted fronts can shift arrival by several minutes.

followups.q: Why no skill score?
followups.a: The feeds carry no archive of earlier forecasts to compare against.
