q: Tell me about your Gravity Spy research.
plain: Since February 2026 you have worked on Gravity Spy 2.0, an NSF funded citizen science project supporting LIGO, building the data pipeline over volunteer classifications of detector glitches and a model trained on paired spectrograms. A glitch is a burst of detector noise that can mimic or hide a real gravitational wave signal. Volunteers sort glitches by looking at spectrograms, pictures of signal strength over time and frequency.
deep: Panoptes API ingestion: 276,000 plus classifications over 23 months; five undocumented metadata schemas across 25,104 glitch subjects and 8,293 auxiliary channels; about 38 science team accounts filtered. OpenCV: 49,000 spectrograms, each 1200 by 1200 mosaic to paired 224 by 224 heatmaps; outputs include a GPS by channel pivot over 455 subsystems. Two input CNN with a shared MobileNetV2 backbone predicting volunteer similarity labels: 0.89 validation AUC on 2,000 held out subjects; ECE 0.10 to 0.05 with label smoothing, AdamW and AUC based early stopping. Descriptives: top ten volunteers make 50 percent of classifications; 52 percent of multiply classified subjects reach perfect consensus.
say: Gravity Spy is NSF funded citizen science that supports LIGO; the science goal is finding which detector subsystems cause the glitches that contaminate gravitational wave data. I built the ingestion on the Zooniverse API: more than 276,000 volunteer classifications over 23 months, which meant reconciling five undocumented metadata schemas across 25,104 glitch subjects, and filtering science team accounts out of the volunteers. I pulled 49,000 spectrograms, turned each into paired channel heatmaps, and trained a two input CNN with a shared MobileNetV2 backbone to predict volunteer similarity labels. It reaches 0.89 validation AUC on 2,000 held out subjects, and calibration error fell from 0.10 to 0.05 with label smoothing, AdamW and AUC based early stopping.

followups.q: Does the model find glitch causes?
followups.a: No, it predicts volunteer similarity labels; causal attribution to subsystems is the science goal it supports.

followups.q: How was the held out set split?
followups.a: Know this: by subject, and whether paired images from the same time could leak across the split.

q: What would an interviewer probe about your Gravity Spy model?
plain: Three things. First, what the labels are: the model predicts volunteer similarity labels, which are noisy human judgements, so it learns what volunteers think, not ground truth, and only 52 percent of subjects classified more than once reach perfect consensus. Second, how the 2,000 subject held out set was split, and whether paired images from the same time or subject could leak across it. Third, why calibration mattered more than AUC, which the portfolio states. Do not claim the model identifies which subsystem causes a glitch; that is the science goal the pipeline supports.

First, what the labels really are: the model predicts volunteer similarity labels, so it learns what volunteers judge, not ground truth, and only 52 percent of subjects seen by more than one volunteer reach perfect agreement, which caps how good any model can look. q: Tell me about the JMA Wireless project.
plain: From January to May 2026 you led a four person Lean Six Sigma team at JMA Wireless, standardised five factory KPIs, made the automated cell measurable, and showed its constraint was upstream material flow rather than the equipment. DMAIC is the Lean Six Sigma sequence Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control. The key move here happened in Define: agreeing what the KPIs meant before measuring anything.
deep: DMAIC over 15 weeks on site, sponsored by the SVP of Global Operations. Define: sponsor approved definitions for Parts per Labor Hour, Uptime, First Time Throughput, Schedule Attainment and a Culture and Engagement index. Measure: pandas json_normalize with explicit record paths, 31 GB raw to under 5 MB. Analyse: cell at 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of weekly target (input limited); manual line at 139.7 percent of its target, hiding the demand signal. Improve: Pugh matrix chose 3 of 6 fixes. Pilot: 2 weeks, red to owner acting about 4 hours to about 25 minutes; KPI familiarity 2.4 to 4.1 of 5. Value: about USD 355,000 a year projected (about 27,000 cables, about 48 analyst hours a week), pending Finance. Control plan with refresh owner and dashboard FMEA.
say: At JMA Wireless, a US maker of 5G infrastructure, I led a four person Lean Six Sigma team for fifteen weeks, sponsored by the SVP of Global Operations. Nobody could compare the manual line with the automated cell, because Uptime and Schedule Attainment meant different things to different functions, so I ran definition interviews and wrote a sponsor approved definition for five KPIs. I also flattened the cell's nested JSON from over 31 gigabytes to under 5 megabytes. Measured the same way, the cell showed 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of its weekly target, so it was starved upstream, not broken. A two week standup pilot cut the median time from a red KPI to an owner acting from about four hours to about twenty five minutes.

followups.q: What was the value?
followups.a: About USD 355,000 a year projected, from roughly 27,000 more cables and 48 analyst hours a week, resting on assumptions JMA Finance still has to confirm.

followups.q: How did you choose fixes?
followups.a: A Pugh matrix over six candidates picked three: a daily standup at a dashboard wall, two bin kitting, and a target reset with a ramp.

traps: Calling the projection a realised saving.
Overselling a two week pilot.

q: Is the JMA Wireless value figure real, and how would you defend the pilot?
plain: Be precise: the roughly USD 355,000 a year is a projected opportunity, not a realised saving. It comes from about 27,000 more cables from the automated line at no extra labour and about 48 analyst hours a week returned from manual reporting, both resting on conservative rate assumptions the team wrote down and that JMA Finance still has to confirm. The pilot was a daily standup run for two weeks, which cut the median time from a red KPI to a named owner acting from about 4 hours to about 25 minutes. Two weeks is short and a novelty effect is possible, and the KPI familiarity score rising from 2.4 to 4.1 is self reported.
deep: Defending the pilot: it measured one specific mechanism (time to action on red status), with a clear before and after on the same team; threats are novelty effects, a small number of events, and no control group; the Control Plan (refresh owner, dashboard FMEA, tiered escalation on red) is what sustains it. Defending the diagnosis rather than the value: 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of weekly target, and the manual line absorbing shortfall at 139.7 percent of its own target, which hid the demand signal from planning.
say: I'd say plainly that the roughly 355,000 dollars a year is a projection, not a saving. It comes from about 27,000 more cables from the automated line with no added labour, plus about 48 analyst hours a week freed from manual reporting, and both rest on rate assumptions we wrote down that JMA Finance still has to confirm. The pilot was a daily standup for two weeks, and the median time from a red KPI to a named owner acting fell from about four hours to about twenty five minutes. Two weeks is short and could include a novelty effect, which is why we handed over a control plan. The part I'd defend hardest is the diagnosis itself.
must_mention: two week pilot, 4 hours to 25 minutes

followups.q: What is the diagnosis you'd defend?
followups.a: 97.3 percent uptime against 46.3 percent of target means the cell was input limited, while the manual line at 139.7 percent of its target hid the shortfall.

traps: Calling the projection savings.

q: Tell me about a time you explained something complex to someone without your background.
plain: Use your cybersecurity TA role: you built and taught 15 plus hands on labs and debugged students' own attack chains in office hours, grading the reasoning as well as the answer. The teaching pattern was to show the same evidence from the attacker's side and then from the defender's side. Asking students to narrate their own steps turned debugging into teaching.
deep: Summer 2025 graduate TA, Syracuse iSchool cybersecurity course. Labs across cryptography (OpenSSL, SHA 256 and SHA 512), network security (Nmap, Wireshark), penetration testing (Metasploit against intentionally vulnerable targets) and digital forensics; attacker workflow then the defender's reading of the same evidence; multi VM environments (Kali against Windows 10, Windows Server, CentOS, Metasploitable) kept reproducible; grading on methodology; scope and authorisation emphasised throughout.
say: As the graduate TA for the iSchool cybersecurity course, I built and taught more than fifteen hands on labs in cryptography, network security, penetration testing and forensics, for students who often had no security background. What worked was teaching each lab twice: first the attacker's workflow, from scanning to exploitation, then flipping to the defender's reading of the same evidence, so the concept stuck from both sides. In office hours I debugged students' own attack chains by asking them to narrate each step, which usually exposed the wrong assumption. I graded the method as well as the answer, because in security the chain of evidence matters as much as the result.
must_mention: grade method as well as answer

followups.q: How did you keep labs reproducible?
followups.a: Maintained the VM images, network configuration and tooling so a whole section ran the same exercise without environment drift.

traps: Making the story about tools instead of how you explained.
